reference_title: Ground Modification Methods Reference Manual – Volume II

sections.title: Description and History
sections.summary: Introduction to Chapter 8: grouting as a set of techniques that introduce materials under pressure to waterproof and/or alter the physical characteristics of soil or rock, its role in transportation infrastructure, and the chapter's purpose as a working guide for preliminary technical and economic evaluation.
sections.body: Grouting comprises a set of geotechnical techniques to introduce materials with pressure, with the objective of waterproofing and/or altering the physical characteristics of the soil or rock formation upon setting (Kutzner 1996). From simple cement slurry injections to today's multi-material techniques, grouting has played an important role in building and upgrading transportation facilities and other infrastructure such as dams, levees and tunnels. Since the late 1990s significant advances have been made across the suite of grouting techniques, as recorded in the ASCE grouting conference proceedings (ASCE 2003, 2004, 2012). New technologies continue to be developed and existing ones refined; with compensation grouting and the progressive refinement of permeation and compaction grouting, grouting now offers a viable, engineered solution to a wide range of problems. The chapter identifies the geotechnical problems grouting can solve and gives the user enough information for a preliminary technical and economic evaluation, on which the potential for a grouting solution may be investigated further. Much published information is hard for the wider engineering community to assimilate, so the chapter is meant as a working guide for strategic decision making. The print stresses that, long as it is, the chapter is only an introduction and engineers embarking on a grouting project are strongly counseled to seek expert advice (p. 8-1).

sections.title: Description
sections.summary: Grouting injects a range of materials into soil or rock via boreholes to fill rock fissures and voids, fill voids under structures, and improve strength, density, permeability or homogeneity; needs thorough investigation, real-time monitoring and verification. Lists the principal types: rock grouting (HMG fissures, LMG voids) and soil grouting methods.
sections.body: Grouting comprises techniques that inject a range of materials into soil or rock formations via boreholes to improve their engineering properties: to fill fissures and voids in rock, to fill voids between the ground and overlying structures, and to treat soils and rocks to enhance strength, density, permeability and/or homogeneity. The method chosen depends on the project's requirements, the soil or rock type and the ground's amenability to different grouts. Integral components of a grouting program are a thorough geotechnical investigation to guide the choice of method, real-time monitoring and analysis of data permitting adjustments, and a responsive verification program (pp. 8-1 to 8-2). Investigations have too often been limited by economics or a failure to recognize their importance; they should be detailed enough to eliminate major surprises, and every hole drilled, exploratory or production, is a source of information about the site. Major components of the investigation include leakage potential, areal and structural geology, in-situ stress, hydrogeology, geochemistry, and compatibility of in-situ and grouting materials. Grout takes, mixes, procedures and pressures are best determined by a grout test program at the site. The principal types (Figure 8-1) are: rock grouting of fissures (High Mobility Grouts, HMG) and of voids (Low Mobility Grouts, LMG), both particulate cement-based grouts; and soil grouting: slabjacking, permeation grouting (particulate, colloidal or solution grouts), low mobility grouting (compaction, displacement and bulk void filling of karst, sinkholes and mines), jet (replacement) grouting, and soil fracture grouting including compensation grouting (p. 8-2).

sections.title: Historical Overview
sections.summary: Grouting has been used in the U.S. since the late nineteenth century: fissure grouting in the 1890s, chemical grouting and compaction grouting (invented in the U.S.) in the 1950s, and soil fracture (compensation) grouting in the 1990s. Figure 8-1 shows schematics of the grouting types.
sections.body: Grouting technologies have been used in the United States since the late nineteenth century, though their invention and use elsewhere began much earlier. The first technology used was fissure grouting in the 1890s, followed by chemical grouting and compaction grouting (invented in the United States) in the 1950s, and soil fracture (compensation) grouting in the 1990s. The historical evolution of the grouting technologies was addressed in the keynote lectures of the International Conference on Grouting (ASCE 2003). Schematics of the various grouting technologies are shown in Figure 8-1 (p. 8-3). The subsections that follow trace the history of rock grouting, slabjacking, permeation, chemical, compaction, jet and soil fracture grouting, each with a list of recommended reading.

sections.title: Rock Grouting
sections.summary: History of rock fissure grouting: hydraulic cut-offs and mechanical binding of rock; pressure grouting invented in 1802; Portland cement grouts from the 1830s; systematic U.S. cavity grouting from 1893 and systematic fissure grouting for a cut-off from 1910; the prescriptive-specification era of dam grouting (1920s-1970s) and later move to performance-type, design-build specifications. Recommended reading list.
sections.body: Rock fissure grouting is mainly used to provide hydraulic cut-offs of relatively low permeability, but can also bind rock masses together mechanically to enhance load-bearing properties. Pressure grouting is credited to an 1802 invention, an 'Injection Process' that used excess pressure to pump a clay and lime suspension to repair deteriorated masonry walls (Houlsby 1990). Portland cement was first used as a grout in 1838 on a tunnel, pressure injection was introduced abroad in 1856, and in 1876 cement grouts were used to inject rock fissures (Karol 2003). It was not until 1893 that pressure grouting appears to have been used systematically to fill cavities (in limestone) under an American structure, a dam (Weaver and Bruce 2007). This was followed by much use of HMGs to repair fissures in masonry bridge piers and other masonry, and in underwater work (preplaced aggregate concrete and tremied foundations), much of it for railroads. Grouting of a dam begun in 1910 is believed to be the first systematic U.S. rock fissure grouting project intended to create a hydraulic cut-off (Houlsby 1990), forerunner of the intense period of dam construction and grouting from the 1920s to the 1970s. Thousands of projects were executed under rigid 'Prescriptive-Type' specifications that standardized approach within, usually federal, owner organizations, at the expense of innovation and foreign input; by the early 1980s American practice was arguably behind practice overseas. Since then specialty contractors, consultants and suppliers, and the demands of dam rehabilitation, have brought significant changes, fostered by 'Performance-Type,' design-build specifications and a better understanding of design rationales (Baker 1985) (pp. 8-4 to 8-6). Recommended reading includes the ASCE proceedings, Houlsby (1990), Kutzner (1996), Lombardi (2003), USACE (1984) and Weaver and Bruce (2007).

sections.title: Slabjacking
sections.summary: Slabjacking (mudjacking) is a subset of void filling: pressure injection of slurry grouts of varying consistency to raise and re-level settled concrete pavements or slabs, also used for under-slab void filling and joint pumping. Practice varies locally; fillers range from fly ash to lime to hot asphalt; proprietary expanding polyurethane foams also used.
sections.body: The term 'slabjacking' (or 'mudjacking') is a subset of void-filling operations and refers to the pressure injection of slurry grouts of varying consistencies to raise and re-level settled concrete pavement or concrete slabs. Slabjacking is also used for under-slab void filling and joint 'pumping.' There is no one typical practice: local belief in what is best for the job seems to be the norm. Slabjacking may use fillers ranging from fly ash to lime to hot asphalt, and grout consistencies ranging from very fluid to zero slump. Certain proprietary processes use expanding polyurethane foams to create uplift pressures and generate movements. Figure 8-2 shows a schematic of the slabjacking process (p. 8-6).

sections.title: Permeation Grouting
sections.summary: Permeation grouting uses particulate, colloidal or solution grouts chosen mainly by soil grain size. Conventional Portland cement grouts permeate only gravels and coarse sands; ultra-fine cement (U.S. 1983) and understanding of pressure filtration and cohesion extended reach, but are no guarantee in medium-fine sands. History of chemical grouts from 1886, the Joosten two-step process, single-shot grouts, acrylamide issues, and sodium silicate's dominance.
sections.body: Permeation grouting uses materials, particulate, colloidal or solution, that can permeate soils, the choice depending largely on the grain size distribution (and hence permeability) of the soil. Because of their particle size, conventional Portland cement grouts can only permeate gravels and coarse sands in properly formulated grouts; in finer soils a filter cake develops at the borehole and stops permeation. Ultra-fine cement was introduced into the United States in 1983, leading to fine-ground cements able to permeate finer sands, and in the 1990s the vital roles of pressure filtration and cohesion in controlling penetrability were better understood (Warner 1999, DePaoli et al. 1992). Ultra-fine cement grouts, even properly formulated and mixed, are alone no guarantee of effective permeation in medium-fine sands (pp. 8-6 to 8-7). Chemical grouting evolved from the limitations of early particulate grouts: large particles, long set times, instability and poor resistance to flowing water. The first chemical grouting patent (1886) injected concentrated sodium silicate in one hole and a coagulant in another; the two-step 'Joosten Process' (1925) injected sodium silicate during pipe placement and calcium chloride during withdrawal. Sodium silicate was the basis of all chemical grouts until the early 1950s (Karol 2003); such two-step processes are now obsolete. 1950s polymer chemistry produced single-shot grouts. After water poisoning linked to acrylamide abroad in 1974, that country banned all chemical grouts except non-toxic silicate grouts; the main U.S. acrylamide maker withdrew the product in 1978, though acrylamides are still in limited use, and acrylates emerged as a replacement for water control. Sodium silicate remains the most widely used grout for soil stabilization (Karol 2003) but is being challenged by ultra-fine cement grouts, while silicate gels are still used in 'borderline' conditions (pp. 8-7 to 8-8).
key_points: Grout choice for permeation depends mainly on soil grain size distribution and permeability

sections.title: Chemical Grouting
sections.summary: Chemical grouting seals water intrusion into tunnels and deep excavations, pretreats coarse soils for tunneling, stabilizes collapsible soils, reduces liquefaction potential and creep. Advantages: no traffic disruption, treats soils down to 4 x 10^-5 in/s permeability to a practical depth of 100 ft. Disadvantages: long durations and set times, cost, toxicity, breakdown with time. Defined as pure-solution grouts (Bruce 2005).
sections.body: Chemical grouting is used to seal off water intrusion into tunnels or deep excavations or to pretreat relatively coarse soils for tunneling. Applications for increasing service life include stabilization of collapsible soils, reduction of liquefaction potential, reduction of creep, and reduced permeability to cut water movement in foundations. Its advantages are the ability to stabilize existing highway structures without traffic disruption, improvement of soils with low permeability (as low as 4 x 10^-5 inches/second) up to a practical depth of 100 feet, and long-lived facilities. Disadvantages are longer design, construction and monitoring durations, long setting times, relatively high cost, high toxicity of some chemicals, and breakdown of the chemical over time reducing its efficiency (p. 8-9). Chemical grouts are defined as any grouting mixture in which all elements of the system are pure solution with no suspended particles (Bruce 2005), ranging from sodium silicate (colloidal) through true solutions such as polyurethanes, resins, acrylates and lignins to exotic precipitation grouts. They are complex, expensive materials typically used only in specialized applications sealing water intrusion into tunnels, deep excavations or through abutments; an exception is sodium silicate grout used to pretreat relatively coarse soils (15% fines or less) for light rail or metro tunneling (pp. 8-9 to 8-10). Cited case uses include sodium silicate underpinning above an existing rail tunnel (Munfakh 1991) and temporary support for a light rail tunnel through sandy outwash (Brachman et al. 2004).
key_points: Uses: sealing water into tunnels/excavations, pretreating coarse soils, collapsible soils, liquefaction, creep, permeability reduction
Treats soils with permeability as low as 4 x 10^-5 in/s up to a practical depth of 100 ft (p. 8-9)

sections.title: Compaction Grouting
sections.summary: Compaction grouting originated in the U.S. in the 1950s to rectify settlements with a very stiff, low-mobility mix; later used preventively during tunneling, for densifying liquefiable soils, karst subsidence and sealing fast flows. Uses low-slump (usually 1 in. or less), high-internal-friction LMG that forms a coherent bulb, compacting the surrounding soil.
sections.body: Compaction grouting was pioneered in the United States in the 1950s and is the only grouting technique originating in the United States. It was first used to rectify structural settlements through controlled injection of a very stiff, low-mobility mix (Warner 1982). In the late 1970s it was used preventively, in lieu of conventional underpinning, to protect surface structures from settlement during tunnel construction (Baker et al. 1983). Recognition that potentially liquefiable soils can be densified led to test programs; a 1985 dam test program showed compaction grouting could be designed to obtain the densification required to improve seismic stability in situ (Baker 1985, Salley et al. 1987). Since the 1980s it has also been used to rectify karst-related subsidence under new and existing structures (Henry 1986, Schmertmann et al. 1986) and as part of processes to seal fast flows (Bruce et al. 2001, Bruce 2003). Compaction grouting uses low-slump (usually 1 inch or less), low-mobility grouts of high internal friction. In weak or loose soils the grout typically forms a coherent 'bulb' at the tip of the injection pipe, compacting and/or densifying the surrounding soil. Injected into loosened areas above tunnels or sinkholes it re-densifies the soil and prevents surface settlement; where settlement has occurred, careful compaction grouting can lift and level structures. Compaction grouts can also be an economic, controllable medium to help fill large voids, even in flowing water (Bruce 1998) (pp. 8-10 to 8-11). A recommended reading list follows (p. 8-11).
key_points: Only grouting technique originating in the U.S. (1950s)
Grout: low slump (usually 1 in. or less), low mobility, high internal friction
Forms a coherent bulb at the pipe tip that compacts/densifies the surrounding soil
Uses: settlement correction, tunneling protection, liquefaction densification, karst subsidence, sealing fast flows, void filling

sections.title: Jet Grouting
sections.summary: Jet grouting was developed in the early 1970s from a 1960s concept, reintroduced abroad in the mid-1970s, and used for underpinning, excavation support, groundwater cut-off and tunneling. U.S. use restarted in 1986 with purpose-built equipment; more than 200 U.S. projects 1988-1997. High-efficiency monitors and nozzles now give larger diameters.
sections.body: Jet grouting was developed in the early 1970s (Yahiro and Yoshida 1972), based on a concept dating from the 1960s. Since its reintroduction abroad in the mid-1970s it has been used extensively for underpinning and/or excavation support of sensitive structures, groundwater cut-off control and tunneling applications (Welsh and Burke 1991, Bell 1993, Bruce 1994, Croce et al. 2014). In the early 1980s in the United States, jet grouting with conventional drilling and grouting equipment was tried on a few demonstration projects; the equipment proved ineffective and the technique went into a hiatus until 1986, when it was reintroduced using equipment specifically designed for it, incorporating contemporary overseas equipment and knowledge. The combination of sophisticated equipment, more technical knowledge and proper applications makes it a successful ground treatment usable with almost any soil type, as shown by more than 200 successful U.S. projects between 1988 and 1997 alone; usage has increased substantially since. Recent advances include high-efficiency tooling (monitors and nozzles) able to produce much higher energy and hence much larger diameters; several such systems are available under various trade names (p. 8-12). A recommended reading list follows (pp. 8-12 to 8-13).
key_points: Developed in the early 1970s (Yahiro and Yoshida 1972)
Uses: underpinning, excavation support, groundwater cut-off, tunneling

sections.title: Soil Fracture Grouting
sections.summary: Soil fracture grouting (U.S. early 1990s) raises settled structures in a highly controlled way and improves load support of soft/loose soils; best in soils that are not free draining. Applications: raising structures, settlement control (compensation grouting during tunneling), underpinning, soil reinforcement (lens grouting, fibers). Costs not well established; specialists should be consulted.
sections.body: Soil fracture grouting was introduced in the United States in the early 1990s. Its primary use is to raise settled or settling structures to their original elevation in a highly controlled manner and to increase the load support of soft and/or loose soils. It works best in soils that are not free draining but can be applied to all soil types. Applications are: raising settled structures, with a high degree of control coupled with instrumentation; settlement control using predesigned fracture injections of particulate slurries, to re-level structures on soft cohesive soils or to maintain structures during tunneling, when it is called 'compensation grouting'; underpinning; and soil reinforcement, where fracture or lens grouting reinforces clayey soils subject to lateral movement and fibers may be added for tensile strength (pp. 8-13 to 8-14). Its cost cannot be accurately gauged because U.S. experience is insufficient; grouting specialists should be contacted for feasibility and cost data. Design of hole spacing, grout type, quantity and equipment is presented in other references (Kramer et al. 1994) and not here. During permeation grouting it was observed that sheets or lenses of grout could be induced to travel from the injection point; such fractures could provide a stiff internal grout skeleton. Developments in the 1970s led to carefully controlled fracturing to compensate for tunneling settlements ('claquage'); by the 1990s compensation grouting with sophisticated construction and monitoring equipment was used in urban soft-ground tunneling (Kramer et al. 1994). Less sophisticated 'lense grouting' (Figure 8-3) has been used for slope stabilization since the late 1980s (Chandler 1997). Specially formulated high-rheology particulate grouts are injected repeatedly through arrays of grout pipes, with parameters controlled in response to the desired surface response (pp. 8-14 to 8-15).
key_points: Primary use: raise settled structures in a highly controlled manner; improve soft/loose soil support
Works best in soils that are not free draining; applicable to all soil types
Compensation grouting = fracture grouting to maintain structures during tunneling
Lens grouting with fibers reinforces clayey soils subject to lateral movement

sections.title: Focus and Scope
sections.summary: States the chapter scope (soil and rock grouting techniques, applications, advantages and disadvantages, feasibility and design considerations, materials and costs) and its six sections: history and glossary; soil and rock grouting techniques with case histories; construction and materials; project planning; specifications and quality assurance; references.
sections.body: This chapter describes soil and rock grouting techniques, their applications, advantages and disadvantages, feasibility and design considerations, suitable grout materials, and costs. It is organized into six sections. Section 1 gives a historic overview of the techniques and a glossary of grouting terminology. Section 2 presents soil and rock grouting techniques such as permeation, low mobility (including compaction, displacement and bulk void filling: karst and sinkhole filling and mine backfilling), jet, rock fissure and other alternate grouting technologies, with further references for in-depth research and project case histories illustrating each technique. Construction methods, drilling and grouting equipment, and grouting materials are presented in Section 3. Project planning activities are described in Section 4. Design considerations, construction methods, specifications, quality assurance and cost data are discussed in Section 5. References used in the chapter are in Section 6 (p. 8-16).
key_points: Six sections: history/glossary, techniques, construction and materials, project planning, specifications/QA, references
Section 2 covers permeation, low mobility, bulk void filling, slabjacking, jet and rock fissure grouting with case histories
sections.applicability: Navigating the chapter to find the right grouting topic.

sections.title: Glossary (or Terminology)
sections.summary: Glossary of U.S. grouting terms, largely from the ASCE Grouting Committee (Bruce 2005): additives, admixtures, Blaine fineness, compaction and compensation grouting, Darcy's law (Eq. 8-1), groutability ratio (D15 soil / D85 grout), LMG, Lugeon, permeation grouting, pressure filtration stability, soilcrete, ultra-fine cement, w/c ratio by volume = 1.5 x by weight.
sections.body: There is no internationally adopted glossary of grouting terms; meanings vary from country to country. The list gives standard U.S. terminology, including many definitions proposed by the ASCE Grouting Committee (Bruce 2005) (p. 8-16). Selected definitions as printed: Blaine is the specific surface of a particulate material; Portland cements have a Blaine value of 1,460-2,440 sq. ft/lb, ultra-fine cements over 3,900 sq. ft/lb and up to 5,370 sq. ft/lb. Colloidal: particles of about 4 x 10^-8 to 4 x 10^-6 inches suspended, not dissolved. Compaction grouting: low-mobility, high-internal-friction grout (LMG) injected with less than 1 inch slump, normally a soil-cement with enough silt for plasticity and enough sand for internal friction; it does not enter soil pores but displaces and compacts loose soils, lifts structures or fills large voids. Compensation grouting: injection concurrent with tunneling to replace lost ground and prevent settlement. Darcy's law (Eq. 8-1). Groutability ratio of granular formations: the ratio of the 15% size of the formation particles to the 85% size of the grout particles (particulate grout) (p. 8-18). LMG grouting: stiff grout that displaces the soil, does not mix with or permeate it and does not travel far; also called limited mobility grouting. Lugeon: 1 L of water per meter of test hole per minute at 10 bars (about 150 psi). Permeation grouting: filling voids at low pressure without destroying the original structure. Soilcrete: cementitious materials mixed with existing soil, as by jet grouting. Solution: particles less than 4 x 10^-8 inches. Stability (pressure filtration): the more water expressed in a standard test, the less stable the grout. Ultra-fine (microfine) cement: finely ground Portland or slag cement. Water/cement ratio: historically by volume in the U.S., increasingly by weight; ratio by volume = 1.5 x ratio by weight (pp. 8-17 to 8-21).
key_points: Groutability ratio of granular formations = 15% size of formation particles / 85% size of grout particles (p. 8-18)
Compaction grout: LMG injected at less than 1 in. slump; does not enter soil pores
One Lugeon = 1 L/m of test hole/min at 10 bars (about 150 psi) (p. 8-19)
Blaine: Portland cement 1,460-2,440 sq. ft/lb; ultra-fine cement over 3,900 and up to 5,370 sq. ft/lb
w/c ratio by volume = 1.5 x ratio by weight (p. 8-21)
True solution: particles less than 4 x 10^-8 in.; colloidal: 4 x 10^-8 to 4 x 10^-6 in.
equations: Eq. 8-1: V = Q/A = K x (dh/dL); Darcy's law, V = velocity (ft/s), Q = flow rate (cu ft/s), A = cross-sectional area (sq ft), K = coefficient of permeability (ft/s), dh/dL = hydraulic gradient (p. 8-17)

sections.title: Soil and Rock Grouting
sections.summary: Introduces Section 2: soil grouting applications and technologies (2.1-2.7) and rock grouting (2.8). Compaction, jet and permeation grouting are well established; soil fracture grouting is newer in the U.S. Fillers such as fly ash, sand and gravel are used in void filling grouts for economy; hot bitumen may be needed to stop high-flow, high-head inflows.
sections.body: This section addresses soil grouting applications and technologies in Sections 2.1 through 2.7 and rock grouting in Section 2.8. Technologies for grouting soils and rock have evolved separately over years of application to a variety of geotechnical problems. Some techniques, such as compaction grouting, jet grouting and permeation grouting, are well established; others, such as soil fracture grouting, are relatively new in the United States. The methods and materials used depend largely on the application and the in-situ geomaterial. For economic reasons alone, fillers such as fly ash, sand and gravel are usually incorporated into void filling grouts (Section 2.5), while other materials such as hot bitumen (Bruce et al. 2001, Bruce and Chuaqui 2012) are necessary to stop high-flow/high-head flows into quarries and/or under dams (p. 8-22).
key_points: Sections 2.1-2.7 cover soil grouting; Section 2.8 covers rock grouting
Compaction, jet and permeation grouting are well established; soil fracture grouting is newer in the U.S.
Void filling grouts usually include fillers (fly ash, sand, gravel) for economy
Hot bitumen may be necessary for high-flow/high-head inflows
sections.applicability: Overview of the soil and rock grouting techniques treated in Section 2.

sections.title: Soil Grouting Applications
sections.summary: Soil grouting divides into grouting for water control and waterproofing (waterproofing for new construction, water control for remedial work) and structural grouting. Permeation, jet, soil fracture and lime injection grouting improve structural strength; LMG grouting serves structural grouting, water control and waterproofing.
sections.body: Soil grouting programs achieve a variety of ground treatment objectives, and a number of techniques are available. Soil grouting can be divided into two major groups of applications: grouting for water control and waterproofing, and structural grouting. Within each class one or more techniques may apply. In this chapter waterproofing refers to new construction and water control to remedial applications. Techniques applicable for structural strength improvement are permeation, jet, soil fracture and lime injection grouting, while LMG grouting can also be used for structural grouting, water control and waterproofing. The major structural applications of soil grouting are summarized in the subsections: densification, raising settled structures, settlement control, underpinning, excavation support, soft-ground tunneling, liquefaction mitigation and water control (p. 8-22).
key_points: Two groups: water control/waterproofing, and structural grouting
Waterproofing = new construction; water control = remedial work (as used in the chapter)
Structural strength: permeation, jet, soil fracture, lime injection grouting
LMG grouting serves structural, water control and waterproofing uses
sections.applicability: Matching a soil grouting technique to the project objective.

sections.title: Densification
sections.summary: Granular soils above and below the water table can be densified by dynamic compaction, vibro-compaction, stone columns and compaction grouting; the others apply only to new construction, and compaction grouting has proven effective for densifying loose granular soils under existing structures.
sections.body: Among the major structural applications of soil grouting, the density of all granular soils above and below the groundwater table can be improved by various in situ techniques, such as dynamic compaction, vibro-compaction, stone columns and compaction grouting. These are only applicable to new construction. For densification of loose granular soils under existing structures, compaction grouting has proven to be effective (p. 8-22).
key_points: Densification options: dynamic compaction, vibro-compaction, stone columns, compaction grouting
Compaction grouting is effective for loose granular soils beneath existing structures
sections.applicability: Densifying loose granular soils, particularly under existing structures.

sections.title: Raising Settled Structures
sections.summary: Raising settled structures needs a controlled grouting operation; HMG grouting has raised slabs and footings but lacks control of the fluid mix, while compaction grouting and soil fracture grouting can be precisely controlled for settlement remediation or compensation.
sections.body: Successful raising of settled structures requires a controlled grouting operation. Although HMG grouting has successfully raised slabs and footings, its major disadvantage is the lack of control of the fluid mixes. Both compaction grouting and soil fracture grouting can be precisely controlled for structural settlement remediation or compensation (p. 8-23).
key_points: Requires a controlled grouting operation
HMG can raise slabs and footings but its fluid mixes are hard to control
Compaction and soil fracture grouting can be precisely controlled
sections.applicability: Selecting a grouting method to lift settled slabs, footings or structures.

sections.title: Settlement Control
sections.summary: Depending on soil type, cost and potential cause of settlement, permeation, compaction, jet and fracture grouting can be effective in controlling post-construction settlement.
sections.body: As a structural application of soil grouting, settlement control depends on the soil type, cost and the potential cause of settlement. Permeation, compaction, jet and fracture grouting can each be effective in controlling post-construction settlement (p. 8-23). It is one of the eight major structural applications of soil grouting summarized in Section 2.1.
key_points: Permeation, compaction, jet and fracture grouting can control post-construction settlement
Choice depends on soil type, cost and cause of settlement
sections.applicability: Controlling post-construction settlement by grouting.

sections.title: Underpinning
sections.summary: A structure is underpinned to prevent settlement from adjacent planned construction or before added foundation loads; depending on the soil, permeation, compaction, jet and soil fracture grouting can be alternatives to other underpinning techniques.
sections.body: A structure is normally underpinned to prevent settlement from occurring due to adjacent planned construction, or when it is proposed to add additional loads to a foundation. Depending on the soil beneath the structure to be underpinned, permeation, compaction, jet and soil fracture grouting can offer alternatives to other underpinning techniques (p. 8-23).
key_points: Underpinning prevents settlement from adjacent construction or added loads
Permeation, compaction, jet and soil fracture grouting are grouting alternatives to conventional underpinning
sections.applicability: Grouting as an underpinning method for existing foundations.

sections.title: Excavation Support
sections.summary: Conventional excavation support uses soldier piles and lagging, sheet piles and diaphragm walls, with or without tiebacks or bracing; where installing these could affect structures or utilities, permeation or jet grouting can be viable alternatives.
sections.body: Soldier piles and lagging, sheet piles and structural diaphragm walls, with or without tiebacks or internal bracing, are the conventional methods of excavation support. However, when structures or utilities can be affected by the installation of these systems, permeation or jet grouting can be viable alternatives (p. 8-23).
key_points: Conventional support: soldier piles and lagging, sheet piles, diaphragm walls
Permeation or jet grouting are alternatives where installing those could affect structures or utilities
sections.applicability: Grouted excavation support near sensitive structures or utilities.

sections.title: Soft-Ground Tunneling
sections.summary: Potential settlement is a design consideration on all soft-ground tunneling projects; permeation, compaction, jet and soil fracture grouting can be effective in preventing or compensating for this settlement.
sections.body: Potential settlement is a design consideration on all soft-ground tunneling projects. Permeation, compaction, jet and soil fracture grouting can be effective in preventing or compensating for this type of settlement (p. 8-23). Compensation grouting, a form of soil fracture grouting, is described in Section 1.2.7.
key_points: Settlement is a design consideration on all soft-ground tunnels
Permeation, compaction, jet and soil fracture grouting can prevent or compensate for it
sections.applicability: Grouting to limit or compensate for tunneling-induced settlement.

sections.title: Liquefaction Mitigation
sections.summary: Where structures are built on soils determined to be liquefiable, permeation, compaction and jet grouting are potential methods for mitigating soils susceptible to liquefaction.
sections.body: Where structures are built on soils that are determined to be liquefiable, permeation, compaction and jet grouting are potential methods for mitigating soils that are susceptible to liquefaction (p. 8-23). Liquefaction mitigation is listed among the major structural applications of soil grouting in Section 2.1; the jet grouting application is described further in Section 2.7.1.6.
key_points: Permeation, compaction and jet grouting are potential liquefaction mitigation methods
sections.applicability: Grouting options for liquefiable soils beneath structures.

sections.title: Water Control
sections.summary: Permeation and jet grouting have proven effective in controlling groundwater infiltration in underground construction; existing structures with water infiltration can often be remediated by permeation, jet grouting and low mobility grouts.
sections.body: Permeation and jet grouting have proven to be effective in controlling groundwater infiltration in underground construction elements, while existing structures experiencing water infiltration can often be remediated by permeation, jet grouting and the use of low mobility grouts (pp. 8-23 to 8-24). Water control is the last of the major soil grouting applications listed in Section 2.1.
key_points: Permeation and jet grouting control groundwater infiltration into underground construction
Existing structures with infiltration: permeation, jet grouting, low mobility grouts
sections.applicability: Grouting for groundwater control in new and existing underground works.

sections.title: Soil Grouting Advantages and Potential Disadvantages
sections.summary: Container section for the advantages (in-situ economy, safety, low disruption) and potential disadvantages (soil-specific techniques, uncertain scope and cost, ground movement) of soil grouting, including Table 8-1 comparing jet grouting systems.
sections.body: This section sets out the advantages and the potential disadvantages of soil grouting in general, and of jet grouting systems in particular, in two subsections (pp. 8-24 to 8-26). The disadvantages subsection includes Figure 8-4, the range of applicability of soil grouting techniques by grain size, and Table 8-1, the advantages and disadvantages of the single-, double- and triple-fluid and higher-energy jet grouting systems.
key_points: Advantages and disadvantages are given in Sections 2.2.1 and 2.2.2
Table 8-1 compares jet grouting systems (p. 8-26)
sections.applicability: Weighing soil grouting against alternatives such as removal and replacement.

sections.title: Advantages
sections.summary: Soil grouting is in situ, so it usually offers an economic advantage over removal and replacement, improves safety (no excavation under structures), and is less disruptive. Notes limits of compaction grouting in fine saturated soils and toxicity of some chemical grouts; jet grouting advantages: unlimited geometry, limited headroom, wide soil range, minimizes settlement.
sections.body: Soil grouting is an in situ treatment and so can usually offer a distinct economic advantage over removal and replacement. Another advantage over removal and replacement is safety: grouting for underpinning requires no excavation beneath structures, eliminating the need for personnel to work in high-risk areas. Grouting is also generally less disruptive to the surroundings, which can be particularly important in residential areas. More sophisticated technologies such as compensation grouting can achieve structural support during tunneling without impeding traffic on existing facilities. The section also notes that in finer, saturated soils the instantaneous pressure of compaction grouting can fail to squeeze pore water out immediately, so densification or consolidation may not be achieved and simple displacement may occur; and that permeation grouting with certain chemical grouts may present toxicity dangers to groundwater, although low-toxicity chemical grouts are now sufficiently available for most purposes and should be specified except in unusual circumstances. Jet grouting has nearly unlimited configurations of column geometry, can be installed in limited headroom, can be used in a wide range of soil types and groundwater conditions, and minimizes settlement (p. 8-24).
key_points: In situ treatment: usually cheaper than removal and replacement
Safer: no excavation beneath structures for underpinning
Less disruptive to surroundings; compensation grouting supports structures during tunneling without traffic impacts
Compaction grouting in fine saturated soils may only displace soil, not densify it
Specify low-toxicity chemical grouts except in unusual circumstances
Jet grouting: nearly unlimited geometry, limited headroom, wide soil range, minimizes settlement
sections.applicability: Arguing the case for an in situ grouting solution.

sections.title: Potential Disadvantages
sections.summary: Individual grouting techniques are limited to specific soils except jet grouting (Figure 8-4); program scope and cost seldom determined accurately in design; effectiveness hard to predict; all methods, especially jet grouting, can cause ground movement; low knowledge outside specialists. Jet grouting disadvantages and Table 8-1 comparing single, double, triple fluid and high-energy systems.
sections.body: Selection of the grouting technology depends heavily on the soil type. Although the range of techniques covers most soil types, individual techniques are limited to specific soils, except jet grouting, as shown in Figure 8-4 (p. 8-24). The full scope and cost of the program can seldom be determined accurately during evaluation or design, and the effectiveness of some applications cannot be predicted with certainty during design. Each grouting method (especially jet grouting) can cause ground movement and structural distress, which must be carefully guarded against. Grouting knowledge is also limited outside specialists. Disadvantages of jet grouting are: installation may cause ground heave; complex equipment; generated spoils must be disposed of or used as fill; and it can be more difficult in plastic soils. Other advantages and disadvantages of the jet grouting systems are in Table 8-1; all systems have problems in very loose soils where the cement travels long distances, especially below the water table (p. 8-25). Table 8-1 (p. 8-26) lists advantages and disadvantages for the single, double and triple fluid systems, the higher-energy proprietary systems and the X-Jet system: the single fluid is simplest but gives the smallest geometry and hardest heave control; the double fluid is most utilized and often most economical but heave control in cohesive soils is very difficult and it is not usually considered for underpinning; the triple fluid is most controllable, gives highest quality in peat and soft clay and is the best underpinning system but is most complex; the higher-energy systems give the lowest cost per volume and largest diameters but need special equipment; the X-Jet gives confidence of geometry and suits soft cohesive soils but needs daily calibration.

Program scope and cost seldom accurately known during design

sections.title: Permeation Grouting
sections.summary: Permeation grouting introduces low-viscosity particulate suspensions or chemical grouts into clean sands, gravels or permeable rock discontinuities without disturbing the ground's structure, to reduce permeability or increase strength. It fills all or most (70% to 80%) of pore spaces; larger pores are filled first with particulate grout, finer pores with chemical or ultra-fine grouts.
sections.body: Permeation grouting is defined as the introduction of low viscosity solutions such as particulate suspensions or chemical grouts into the ground, e.g., clean sands and gravels or permeable discontinuities in rock, without disturbing the structure of the ground (Littlejohn 2003). It is used to reduce permeability or increase strength of the soil, or make the original soil mass more homogeneous and cohesive (p. 8-26). The grout type depends on the grain size of the in-situ soil and the desired results (Figure 8-4). 'Structural permeation grouting' improves the strength and/or rigidity of groutable soils to prevent ground collapse, reduce unacceptable construction movement or improve bearing capacity; 'waterproof grouting' aims primarily at stopping the flow of water. Underpinning is another structural application, in which granular foundation soils are strengthened to permit excavation adjacent to footings. Permeation grouting is intended to fill all (or most, i.e., 70% to 80% of) the natural pore spaces without changing the virgin structure or volume, increasing cohesion between particles and so strength, and/or reducing permeability. As a general rule the finer the pores, the higher the cost of the grout; so it is normal to fill larger pores first with conventional particulate grouts and to permeate finer or residual pores with chemical or ultra-fine grouts (p. 8-27).
key_points: Introduces low-viscosity grout into the ground without disturbing its structure (Littlejohn 2003)
Structural permeation grouting vs. waterproof grouting
Intended to fill all or most (70% to 80%) of natural pore spaces (p. 8-27)
Finer pores cost more to grout: fill large pores with particulate grout first, then chemical or ultra-fine grout
sections.applicability: Permeation grouting of granular soils or permeable rock for strength or water cut-off.

sections.title: Applications
sections.summary: Permeation grouting applications: waterproofing (subway tunnels, mines, diaphragm walls), seepage control, slope stabilization, soil strengthening to reduce lateral support, settlement control/underpinning/excavation support in granular soils, soft-ground tunneling (Figure 8-5), and liquefaction mitigation.
sections.body: Permeation grouting is used to improve the characteristics of soils, for the following applications: waterproofing, typically for remedial purposes such as subway tunnels, sealing off water ingress in mining (Littlejohn 2003) and vertical diaphragm walls (Town 2012); seepage control; slope stabilization; soil strengthening to reduce lateral support requirements (Mitchell 1981); settlement control, underpinning and excavation support of granular soils during excavation; soft ground tunneling, to increase cohesion, as shown in Figure 8-5; and mitigating the need for liquefaction retrofit by increasing density and displacing pore water (pp. 8-27 to 8-28).
key_points: Waterproofing (remedial), seepage control, slope stabilization
Soil strengthening to reduce lateral support requirements (Mitchell 1981)
Settlement control, underpinning and excavation support in granular soils
Soft-ground tunneling support (Figure 8-5); liquefaction mitigation

sections.title: Feasibility Evaluations
sections.summary: Feasibility of permeation grouting: fines limits (readily groutable <12%, moderately 12-15%, marginally 15-20%, ungroutable >20%); groutability ratios N = (D15)soil/(D85)grout (Eq. 8-2) and Nc = (D10)soil/(D95)grout (Eq. 8-3): grouting consistently possible if N > 24 or Nc > 11, not possible if N < 11 or Nc < 6; cement-type soil size limits; Hazen's equation (Eq. 8-4); permeability-based injectability ranges.
sections.body: Feasibility depends on soil type, stratigraphy, site history, soil permeability, grout properties and effects on groundwater. A 'groutable' soil accepts a given grout under practical pressures at an economical flow rate (p. 8-28). Geotechnical (2.3.2.1): particulate grouts permeate only coarse soils such as medium to coarse sands and gravels. Sand permeability may vary three or four orders of magnitude, from 0.4 in/s for medium clean sands to 4 x 10^-5 in/s for sand with 25% or more silts and clays; permeation grouting is recommended only in predominantly sandy materials with less than 15% silts and clays. Soils are readily groutable with less than 12% fines, moderately groutable at 12-15%, marginally groutable at 15-20%, and usually ungroutable above about 20% fines. Groutability ratios (King and Bush 1963), supported by De Paoli et al. (1992) for stable, low-cohesion grouts, are given by Eq. 8-2 and 8-3: grouting is consistently possible if N > 24 or Nc > 11, and not possible when N < 11 or Nc < 6 (p. 8-29). Soil sizes: Type I and II Portland cement, soils coarser than 0.024 in.; Type III, coarser than 0.016 in.; bentonite, coarser than 0.01 in.; microfine cement, coarser than 0.002 in. Hazen's equation (Eq. 8-4) approximates injectability (Lees and Chuaqui 2003). Landry et al. (2000), with small-scale field testing recommended: readily groutable 0.04 >= k >= 4 x 10^-4 in/s; marginally 4 x 10^-4 to 4 x 10^-5; practically ungroutable 4 x 10^-5 to 4 x 10^-6; regular cement k > 0.04, microfine cement k > 0.002, solution grouts k > 4 x 10^-5 in/s. Chemical permeation is most effective below 10% fines, less effective above 15%, not possible above 20% (p. 8-30). Environmental (2.3.2.2): early acrylamide incidents led to bans on all but non-toxic silicate grouts. Project conditions (2.3.2.3): gradually thickening mixes from w/c 2.0 used after 1991; dilute unstable mixes at w/c 4.0 to 8.0 were needed in deep, hot mines (p. 8-31).

sections.title: Design Considerations
sections.summary: Permeation grouting design: clear quantitative objectives; permanence of grouts (silicates not permanent); grout pipe spacing 1.6-5 ft for waterproofing and 3.3-5.2 ft for structural (typical 4 ft); sleeve-port pipes (tubes-a-manchette); grout volume from porosity (0.25-0.45; 350 L per m3 at 0.35) plus 5-15% for edge dilution; pumps and chemical handling; grout types, w/c 0.5-6, silicate 25-30% (waterproofing) or 40-60% (structural).
sections.body: Clear, quantitative objectives are a prerequisite. A program needs a suitable grout, drilling equipment, procedures and hole pattern; a structural objective is often to give non-cohesive ground enough cohesion to prevent collapses or runs into excavations, tunnels or shafts. Many grouts (including properly formulated particulate grouts) are permanent (service life over 20 years), but most structural chemical grouting is needed for only days to months, and sodium silicate grouts cannot be regarded as permanent (Naudts 1995, Baker 1982) (p. 8-31). Hole spacing can be designed from equations (Xanthakos et al. 1994); for preliminary work: Spacing (2.3.3.1) 1.6 to 5 ft for waterproofing and 3.3 to 5.2 ft for structural use, typically 4 ft. Equipment (2.3.3.2): sleeve-port pipes ('tubes-a-manchette', Figure 8-7) should be used on all permeation projects: a 1- to 2-in. plastic pipe with ports usually on 1-ft centers under rubber sleeves, set in a brittle cement-bentonite sheath, injected bottom-up with a double packer and re-injectable. Grout bulbs are commonly elliptical, height to diameter about 0.80, since horizontal exceeds vertical permeability (pp. 8-32 to 8-33). Grout quantities (2.3.3.3): groutable soils have porosities of 0.25 to 0.45; at 0.35 porosity, 350 liters (92.5 gal) of grout per cubic meter of soil; porosity may be split, e.g., 10% particulate and 25% chemical; add 5% to 15% for 'edge dilution' (p. 8-33). Construction equipment (2.3.3.4): continuous mixing plant with set time 5 to 50 minutes, pressure and rate sensors, 'Y' fitting with check valves, tanks for one day of material (p. 8-34). Grout types (2.3.3.5): chemical or particulate; cement particle size, viscosity and pressure filtration coefficient control effectiveness; w/c 0.5 to 6; soil-cement ratio 4 to 6 by volume with w/c 0.33 to 2; silicate 25-30% for waterproofing, 40-60% for structural strength (p. 8-35; Figure 8-8).

sections.title: Cost
sections.summary: Preliminary permeation grouting quantity and cost: ground volume (cu yd) x 30% grout factor, converted to quarts (x 808); sodium silicate in place about $0.65 per quart ($2.50/gal) above 200,000 quarts; add mobilization $10,000-$50,000 and sleeve-port pipes from $20 per linear foot.
sections.body: To make a preliminary estimate of permeation grouting quantities, the volume of ground to be treated (cubic yards) is multiplied by a projected 30% grout volume factor, and this volume is converted to quarts by multiplying by 808. For a project where more than 200,000 quarts of sodium silicate grout are anticipated, a cost of $0.65 per quart ($2.50/gallon) in place can be used for estimating. A mobilization/demobilization rate of $10,000 to $50,000, and a cost of providing and installing the sleeve-port grout pipes starting at a minimum of $20 per linear foot, should be added to the estimate. This preliminary estimate would be applicable for any particulate permeation grouting (p. 8-36).
key_points: Grout quantity = ground volume (cu yd) x 0.30, x 808 to convert to quarts
Sodium silicate in place: $0.65/quart ($2.50/gal) for > 200,000 quarts

sections.title: Case Histories
sections.summary: Two permeation grouting case histories: (1) multiple-pass permeation grouting with stable cement-based suspensions and an acrylamide curtain to encapsulate liquid low-level radioactive waste in trenches, reducing hydraulic conductivity by up to five orders of magnitude (Naudts et al. 2012); (2) field trials of sodium silicate, microfine powder and microfine cement in outwash sands for tunnel support (Brachman et al. 2004).
sections.body: Case History 1: Multiple pass permeation grouting to encapsulate and contain radioactive waste (Naudts et al. 2012). The program hydraulically isolated 34 million quarts of liquid low-level radioactive waste in two trenches (one 295 ft long by 15.7 ft deep; the other three cells 98 ft long by 15.7 ft deep) for a target of 200 years. Multiple-pass, multiple-stage, multiple-hole permeation grouting through driven steel sleeve pipes used five stable, balanced cement-based suspension mixes (Class F fly ash, pre-hydrated biopolymer to cut pressure filtration, superplasticizer), and an acrylamide curtain was built in the surrounding soil; work was monitored by a computer-aided grout evaluation system after a verification trench. Lugeon values dropped to zero after 4 to 5 passes; hydraulic conductivity fell by up to five orders of magnitude in the crushed stone (4 x 10^-3 to 4 x 10^-8 in/s) and two orders in the soil (4 x 10^-5 to 4 x 10^-7 in/s), below the 4.0 x 10^-6 in/s target (pp. 8-36 to 8-37). Case History 2: Permeation grouting in outwash sands (Brachman et al. 2004). Field trials compared sodium silicate, microfine powder and microfine cement for temporary support of sandy soil for two 20.33-ft-diameter light rail tunnels (Figure 8-9). Fines varied from 1% to 28%: 11 of 13 samples readily groutable, one moderately and one not groutable. Twelve holes at 4 ft center-to-center on a triangular grid, depths 34.5 to 45 ft, with mixes per Table 8-2. Seismic velocity after four days showed microfine cement (very high injection pressures) gave a non-uniform mass, microfine powder gave no strength gain even after a month (low temperature, lack of oxygen, poor mixing), and sodium silicate was most successful, giving a well-permeated hard soil mass (pp. 8-37 to 8-39).

sections.title: Compaction Grouting / LMG Grouting
sections.summary: LMG (limited mobility) grouting injects a stiff grout that does not mix with or penetrate the soil, often displaces it, and does not travel far from the injection point (Byle 1997); low-slump LMG injected into loose or loosened soils, or into rock voids as bulk infill or in seepage remediation.
sections.body: Low mobility grout (LMG) grouting is defined as 'the injection of a stiff grout that does not mix with or penetrate the soil, often displaces the substrate into which it is injected, and does not travel very far from the point of injection' (Byle 1997). It is also known as limited mobility grouting. It consists of the injection of low slump, low mobility grout into loose or loosened soils of appropriate grain size distribution. Alternatively, similar LMGs can be injected into voids in rock masses as a bulk infill material or as a component of a seepage remediation grouting program; bulk infill grouting is presented in Section 2.5 (p. 8-39).
key_points: LMG: stiff grout that does not mix with or penetrate the soil and does not travel far (Byle 1997)
Also called limited mobility grouting
Injected into loose/loosened soils, or into rock voids as bulk infill or for seepage remediation
sections.applicability: Compaction (low mobility) grouting of loose soils and voids.

sections.title: Applications
sections.summary: LMG applications: compaction grouting, sealing flowing channels, pre-grouting large fractures before fissure grouting, abandoned mine filling, structural grout columns (underpinning), grout jacking, soil reinforcement, post-grouting deep foundations. Uses include settlement correction, densification (static and seismic), underpinning, ground strengthening near excavations or tunnels, settlement control over tunnels or sinkholes (Figure 8-10), and sealing major water ingress.
sections.body: LMG is used in the following applications: compaction grouting; sealing of flowing channels, by injecting LMG with water reducing and viscosity modifying admixtures for cohesiveness and washout resistance; pre-grouting of large fractures, to reduce opening sizes and make subsequent high mobility rock (fissure) grouting more effective; abandoned mine filling, to prevent or remediate collapse; structural supports, grout columns to underpin buildings and other structures; grout jacking beneath slabs or structures that have settled; soil reinforcement; and post-grouting of deep foundations (p. 8-39). Uses of compaction/LMG grouting include correction of differential settlement and raising of surface structures; soil densification for static and seismic enhancement; structural underpinning; ground strengthening adjacent to open excavation or tunneling; settlement control over tunnels or sinkholes, as shown in Figure 8-10; and sealing off major water ingress through open channel systems (p. 8-40).

Abandoned mine filling, structural grout columns, grout jacking
Soil reinforcement and post-grouting of deep foundations

sections.title: Feasibility Evaluations
sections.summary: Compaction grouting feasibility rests on a specialty contractor's input and a test program; no equations exist to design spacing, rates or volumes, but much case experience guides practice. Effective in free-draining soils (gravels, sands, coarser silts), not economical in fine-grained soils; grout needs high internal friction; slump up to 3 in. for void filling. Site assessment by SPT, CPT and geophysics.
sections.body: As in all specialty geotechnical processes, a specialty contractor's input should be sought starting with a well-conceived test program, especially when the purpose is to raise a settled structure or compensate for ground loosening beneath a structure next to soft-ground tunneling. There are no mathematical equations to accurately design grout hole spacing, rates of injection, limiting volumes and so on, as there are for permeation grouting; there is, however, much documented project experience (pp. 8-40 to 8-41). Geotechnical (2.4.2.1): densification by compaction grouting may be expected to be effective in all relatively free-draining soils, including gravels, sands and coarser silts; in fine-grained soils pore pressures may not dissipate and improvement may not be economical. The grout must have high internal friction so the bulbs keep their 'spheroidal' shape; otherwise fracturing and lensing make densification ineffective (Warner et al. 1992). For LMG used to fill voids or cut off water, a slightly higher slump (up to 3 inches) or polypropylene fibers may be preferable. Environmental (2.4.2.2): minimal adverse impact because the grout is confined to its zone of influence; computer-controlled directional drilling and injection control and imaging improve precision. Project conditions (2.4.2.3): SPT and CPT are typically used for site assessment; for sinkholes or flow sealing, piezometric data and geophysics (GPR, resistivity, electromagnetic imaging, tomography) give wider coverage; access must always be considered (p. 8-41).

No equations exist for compaction grouting spacing, rates or volumes; design relies on experience

sections.title: Design Considerations
sections.summary: Compaction grouting design: pipe spacing 8-15 ft (tunneling), 6.6-16 ft (site improvement), 3.3-10 ft (remedial under structures), 10-30 ft primaries for sinkholes; pipe at least 3 in.; LMG volume 3-12% of treated soil; pug mixer and pumps from 1/2 cu ft/min; stages 1-3 ft; mixes of 3-6 sacks cement per cu yd silty sand, 10-25% fines, max 1 in. slump; injection 1.5-2.0 cu ft/min, perimeter first.
sections.body: Spacing (2.4.3.1): for densification or re-densification, grout pipes are typically at 8 to 15 ft intervals for tunneling, 6.6 to 16 ft for site improvement, and 3.3 to 10 ft for remedial work on existing structures; primary holes for locating and sealing sinkholes or channel flows are typically 10 to 30 ft, usually with tertiary holes to verify performance. The pipe diameter should be at least 3 inches to carry low-slump grout without plugging (pp. 8-41 to 8-42). Grout quantities (2.4.3.2): for most densification projects the LMG volume ranges from 3 to 12% of the soil volume treated; void filling stages may take tens of cubic meters. Construction equipment (2.4.3.3): mixers, pumps and hoses per Warner (1982); pumps must inject from 1/2 cu ft/min upward; a pug mixer gives uniform mixing; ready-mix delivery is possible if each load meets the slump criterion; site batching gives more control. Grout pipes are steel casing; grout is injected while withdrawing the pipe in stages typically 1 to 3 ft (p. 8-42). Grout types (2.4.3.4): soil-cement mixes with low w/c (Mitchell 1981); zero-slump LMG from cement, clay and fly ash; Type I or II Portland cement; sand with not less than 10% and not more than 25% fines; about three to six sacks of cement per bulk cubic yard of silty sand, with not more than 1 in. slump at the header; gravel, fibers or anti-washout agents as needed; no cement where a 'hard point' must be avoided, as in a dam core. Grout injection (2.4.3.5): optimal rate usually 1.5 to 2.0 cu ft/min (Warner and Byle 2012); excessive rates build pore pressure, can damage structures and reduce the improved radius; use slower rates near walls, slopes and embankments; inject perimeter holes before interior holes (p. 8-43).
key_points: Pipe spacing: 8-15 ft tunneling, 6.6-16 ft site improvement, 3.3-10 ft remedial; 10-30 ft sinkhole primaries (p. 8-41)
Grout pipe diameter at least 3 in. (p. 8-42)
LMG volume typically 3-12% of treated soil volume
Stages typically 1-3 ft; pumps from 1/2 cu ft/min
Mix: 3-6 sacks cement per cu yd silty sand, sand fines 10-25%, slump not more than 1 in. (p. 8-43)
Injection rate usually 1.5-2.0 cu ft/min (Warner and Byle 2012); grout perimeter holes first

sections.title: Cost
sections.summary: LMG grouting uses a split-spaced grid; costs vary from about $5.00 to more than $50.00 per cubic yard of soil treated plus mobilization and pipe installation; grout alone $60-$120 per cubic yard; sensitive to price fluctuation.
sections.body: A split-spaced grid pattern is used, with grid spacing and injected volume dependent on the required increase in density or the size of the void to be filled. As a result, LMG grouting costs vary from as low as $5.00 per cubic yard of soil treated to more than $50.00 per cubic yard, plus mobilization and pipe installation costs. Variation in projects, drilling costs, mixtures, quantity injected, rate of injection and so on makes the system particularly sensitive to price fluctuation. The cost of the grout alone is in the range of $60 to $120 per cubic yard (p. 8-43).
key_points: Split-spaced grid pattern
$5.00 to > $50.00 per cu yd of soil treated, plus mobilization and pipe installation
Grout alone $60-$120 per cu yd
sections.applicability: Order-of-magnitude cost of compaction/LMG grouting.

sections.title: Case Histories
sections.summary: Three compaction grouting case histories under roadways: (1) stabilizing settlement of a fill and rock-armored slope over a failed culvert, with volumetric seismic imaging for QA (Haramy et al. 2012); (2) bottom-up compaction grouting of a loose embankment beneath a subsiding highway; (3) combined void-fill and compaction grouting of piped roadway fill (Lynch et al. 2011), leading to a seismic-velocity pay factor (Eq. 8-5, Table 8-4).
sections.body: Case History 1 (Haramy et al. 2012): compaction grouting stabilized roadway settlement (over 4 in. per year) caused by piping from a failed 2-ft culvert through a 65-ft-high, 131-ft-long rock armored slope. The culvert was lined, armor voids were grouted, and the fill was densified with holes on four longitudinal lines 6.5 ft apart, holes at 13.1 ft staggered 6.5 ft (Figure 8-11), to bedrock at 6.5 to 30 ft, grouted bottom-up in 1-ft lifts. A volumetric seismic method (High Definition Imaging) monitored grout propagation in near real time as QA (pp. 8-44 to 8-45). Case History 2 (Lynch et al. 2011): loose embankment and voids under a highway; staggered holes at 4 ft to 10 ft depth, about 4 ft from the edge, in poorly graded fine sand with SPT 5 to 14; maximum slump 1.8 in.; two sites took 79 and 107 holes and 4.2 and 15.3 cu yd. Near-surface grouting produced a 'pitcher's mound' effect from low overburden; measured slump may not reflect the grout's stress state under pumping (pp. 8-45 to 8-46). Case History 3 (Lynch et al. 2011): void-fill plus compaction grouting of piped roadway fill, pipes 2 to 17 ft deep, w/c 0.77 by weight (1.17 by volume), mix in Table 8-3. Both cases called for 3D seismic tomography guidelines (same locations for geophones and sources, same starting velocity, distant benchmarks, straight parallel lines, planar layout) and led to a pay factor based on the Seismic Volume Improvement Factor (Eq. 8-5): pay factor 0.90 for SVIF < -100, 0.95 for -100 to -50, 1.0 for -50 to 50, 1.10 for 50 to 100, and 1.20 for SVIF > 100 (Table 8-4) (pp. 8-46 to 8-48).
key_points: Case 1: hole lines 6.5 ft apart, holes 13.1 ft on line, staggered 6.5 ft; 1-ft lifts (p. 8-44)
Case 2: maximum slump 1.8 in.; 'pitcher's mound' effect near the surface (p. 8-46)
Case 3: mix w/c 0.77 by weight (1.17 by volume) (Table 8-3)
equations: Eq. 8-5: SVIF = [sum over j=1..n of dv_j] / (n x v_mean,pre-grouting) x 100%; Seismic Volume Improvement Factor, dv_j = velocity change at data point j between pre- and post-grouting, n = number of data points, v_mean,pre-grouting = mean pre-grouting velocity (p. 8-47)

sections.title: Bulk Void Filling
sections.summary: Bulk void filling uses large quantities of cement-based grout to fill subsurface voids such as karstic cavities in soluble rock or man-made cavities such as mines; the whole cavity can be filled, or low-slump grout columns built to reinforce the void roof.
sections.body: Bulk void filling is a process in which large quantities of cement-based grout are used to fill subsurface voids such as karstic cavities in soluble rock or manmade cavities such as mines. The entire cavity can be filled, or low slump grout columns can be constructed to reinforce the roof of the void (p. 8-48). The subsections cover applications, advantages and potential disadvantages, feasibility evaluations, design (grout types and selection, design procedure, performance monitoring), cost data and four case histories.
key_points: Large volumes of cement-based grout fill karst cavities or mines
Either fill the whole cavity or build low-slump grout columns to support the roof
sections.applicability: Filling karst cavities, sinkholes and abandoned mines with grout.

sections.title: Applications
sections.summary: Bulk void filling applications: karstic limestone cavity infill, backfilling old mineral workings, and repair of scour under bridges. LMG injected into limestone cavities seals them and re-densifies loosened overburden, preventing sinkholes, even in flowing water; drilling and grouting commonly fills collapsed or abandoned coal and iron mines to prevent subsidence.
sections.body: Bulk void filling is employed in a large array of applications, including karstic limestone cavity infill, backfilling of old mineral workings, and repair of scour problems under bridges. Many regions of the United States are underlain by limestone, which tends to erode and dissolve over time, forming in-situ cavities; these 'sinkholes' can cause the ground above to collapse or sink if they migrate to the surface. LMGs can be injected into the cavities to seal them and re-densify the loosened overburden soil. The rheology of the grout prevents it from flowing through the network of caverns that can exist in limestone, so localized filling and stabilization of an area can be accomplished and sinkholes prevented. Depending on grout design and site, this approach can also be used in flowing water (Bruce et al. 1998, Bruce et al. 2001, Bruce 2003). Drilling and grouting are commonly used to fill collapsed or abandoned coal and iron mines to prevent surface subsidence, a major application in several states (ASCE 2003) (p. 8-48).
key_points: Applications: karst cavity infill, backfilling old mineral workings, bridge scour repair
LMG seals limestone cavities and re-densifies loosened overburden
Grout rheology keeps it from flowing through cavern networks; usable even in flowing water
Abandoned coal and iron mines filled to prevent subsidence
sections.applicability: Uses of bulk void filling in karst, mines and scour holes.

sections.title: Advantages and Potential Disadvantages
sections.summary: Bulk void filling is usually economical and often the only viable solution; drilling and grouting extend the exploration program. Advantages: low unit cost with cheap fillers, minimal disturbance, tailored strength, full roof contact, verifiable. Disadvantages: difficulty filling voids completely and containing grout in the target zone (barriers, accelerated grouts, fabric forms, Figure 8-12).
sections.body: Advantages (2.5.2.1): bulk void filling is usually an economical way to solve these problems and, on many occasions, is the only viable solution when a void or cavity affects surface structures. As with other grouting, the drilling and grouting should be considered an extension of the exploration program while also remediating the problem. Advantages are: low cost per unit volume of materials when inexpensive fillers are used; minimum disturbance of existing surface structures; grout strength can be tailored to the in-situ condition; it essentially yields full roof contact; grout can penetrate all locations without fear of the grout flowing, settling or being washed away; and effectiveness can be verified (p. 8-49). Potential disadvantages (2.5.2.2): two challenges are common. One is the difficulty of filling the voids completely with grout; the second is containing the grout within the zone to be stabilized, although low-slump grout 'barriers,' accelerated grouts and grout-filled fabric forms have been used to minimize this problem, as illustrated in Figure 8-12 (pp. 8-49 to 8-50).
key_points: Usually economical; often the only viable solution for voids affecting structures
Drilling and grouting are an extension of the exploration program
Advantages: low unit cost with fillers, little disturbance, tailored strength, full roof contact, verifiable
Challenges: filling voids completely and containing grout in the target zone
Containment aids: low-slump grout barriers, accelerated grouts, grout-filled fabric forms

sections.title: Feasibility Evaluations
sections.summary: Void filling feasibility uses historical as-built and mine maps (related to present landforms), visual or underground assessment where safe, and in karst intensive exploration drilling with geophysics (GPR, resistivity) and hydrological tests. Design needs the lateral and vertical extent of voids and the groundwater regime, including flow location, velocity and rate.
sections.body: As in all grouting, available information should be considered before feasibility is established. For void filling it should include historical as-built data on mine and tunnel projects. Historical mine maps are an invaluable source but must be related to contemporary land forms or structures, and can be supplemented by visual surface or underground assessment where man-access is practical and safe. Karstic terrain is often more difficult to assess and may involve intensive exploration drilling, usually supplemented by geophysical (e.g., GPR, resistivity) and hydrological tests; great variability may be expected between adjacent boreholes in karst. As a basis for design, the lateral and vertical extent of the voids or collapsed zones must be determined together with the groundwater regime, in particular whether water is flowing, where, and at what velocity and rate. Projects involving several hundred holes to depths greater than 300 ft and grouts formulated from hundreds of thousands of tons of materials are not uncommon (pp. 8-50 to 8-51).
key_points: Use historical as-built data and mine maps, related to present landforms
Karst needs intensive exploration drilling plus geophysics (GPR, resistivity) and hydrological tests
Design needs extent of voids and whether, where and how fast groundwater flows
Projects of several hundred holes deeper than 300 ft are not uncommon
sections.applicability: Investigations needed before designing a void filling program.

sections.title: Design Overview
sections.summary: Void filling design: grout materials range from non-cementitious waste to high-strength low-slump concrete; scour repair with filled tubes or bags uses a fine aggregate concrete (Table 8-5: cement 37-47, fly ash 11-14, sand 134-144, water 33-37 lb/cu ft). Remove clay infill first; intermittent grouting with 30-1,000 cu ft or more per period; split spacing to refusal, final grid 10 ft or less; monitoring by borehole cameras, instruments and volume/pressure analysis.
sections.body: Grout types and selection (2.5.4.1): materials range from non-cementitious waste to high-strength, low-slump concrete depending on purpose; void filling usually encompasses other grouting techniques, so the LMG, fissure grouting and HMG sections should be reviewed. For scoured zones filled with concrete-filled tubes or bags, a fine aggregate concrete (structural grout) is recommended, with typical proportions in Table 8-5: cement 37-47 lb/cu ft (650-750 kg/m3), fly ash 11-14 (180-220), sand 134-144 (2150-2300), water 33-37 (525-600) (p. 8-51). Design procedure (2.5.4.2): good grouting practice can fill voids completely, but clay or other erodible infill is best removed first by flushing with air, water and/or dispersant; trapped clay can be removed under prolonged differential head. The extent of a cavity is unknown after one grout hole, and geophysics may not help. Intermittent grouting (inject, wait several hours, inject again) may be needed; the maximum quantity per injection period varies from about 30 to 1,000 cu ft or more, and a limit per hole may be set, unlike fissure grouting practice. At refusal the cavity portion penetrated is assumed filled; further holes are drilled on a split spacing until results are achieved. If pressures do not build or the cavity is too large, a grout curtain should contain the grout, or different materials and methods (foams, accelerators, cutoff diaphragms or formed walls, hot bitumen, excavation, grout-filled bags) considered. Final grids of 10 ft or less are not unusual for 'tightening' (pp. 8-51 to 8-52). Performance monitoring (2.5.4.3): borehole cameras in adjacent holes, instruments for heave and settlement, geophysics, and above all close analysis of grout volumes and pressures in each phase (p. 8-52).
key_points: Scour repair fine aggregate concrete (Table 8-5): cement 37-47, fly ash 11-14, sand 134-144, water 33-37 lb/cu ft
Remove clay or erodible infill by flushing with air, water and/or dispersant before grouting
Intermittent grouting: about 30 to 1,000 cu ft or more per injection period (p. 8-52)
Split-spaced holes to refusal; final grid of 10 ft or less not unusual
If pressure does not build, contain grout with a curtain or change materials/methods
Monitor with borehole cameras, heave/settlement instruments and grout volume/pressure records

sections.title: Cost Data
sections.summary: Void filling costs: primary grid 10-100 ft on center; drill holes 3.0-8.0 in. diameter from $7.00 per linear foot; grout supply, mixing and injection about $57-$153 per cu yd; scour repair with concrete fabric forms (1968-1976) $230-$765 per cu yd (Okonkwo et al. 1998); mobilization of a single drill and grout plant under $15,000.
sections.body: In most void filling projects, overburden and rock must be penetrated to reach the voids. Primary, secondary and sometimes tertiary hole spacing is normally used, with the primary grid ranging from 10 to 100 ft on center. Drill hole diameter normally ranges from 3.0 to 8.0 inches and cost starts at $7.00 per linear foot. The cost for supplying, mixing and injecting the grout normally ranges between 57 and $153 per cubic yard. A review of bridge scour repair using concrete fabric forms from 1968 to 1976 in one state indicates $230 to $765 per cubic yard (Okonkwo et al. 1998) (p. 8-52). Void filling costs comprise mobilization and demobilization; drilling (production and exploratory); flushing and water testing; mixing and injecting grouts; materials; and verification drilling and testing. Mobilization varies with the number and complexity of drill rigs and grout plants; a single drill and grout plant should be under $15,000 (p. 8-53).
key_points: Primary hole grid 10 to 100 ft on center
Drill holes 3.0-8.0 in. diameter, from $7.00 per linear ft
Grout supplied, mixed and injected: about $57-$153 per cu yd
Concrete fabric form scour repair: $230-$765 per cu yd (Okonkwo et al. 1998)
Mobilization of one drill and grout plant under $15,000 (p. 8-53)
sections.applicability: Order-of-magnitude cost of bulk void filling.

sections.title: Case Histories
sections.summary: Four bulk void filling case histories: (1) sinkhole remediation under roads with sand/cement/fly ash grout and foamed grout (McGillivray et al. 2012); (2) hot bitumen with LMG and HMG to stop a high-flow quarry inflow (Bruce and Chuaqui 2012); (3) seepage cutoff in karstic limestone with LMG, bitumen and MPSP grouting (Walz et al. 2003); (4) abandoned coal mine filling with LMG barrier and HMG infill (Greenwood and Hill 2012).
sections.body: Case History 1 (McGillivray et al. 2012): road sinkholes in karst under 30 to 60 ft of sand or clayey sand over 5 to 20 ft of plastic clay over porous limestone (Figure 8-13). Grout holes into the limestone 5 ft apart in three rows beyond the sinkhole, 13 pipes at 46 to 77 ft; one 2003 job took 408 cu yd of grout costing $45,000, about two-thirds of the total. Adding foam (grout-foam 60 to 40) saved about 20 to 25%; foamed grout strength was 290 psi versus about 4000 psi (p. 8-54). Case History 2 (Bruce and Chuaqui 2012): two conduits about 20 x 30 ft at 250 and 305 ft depth carried a 35,000 gal/min inflow to a quarry floor more than 330 ft deep (Figure 8-14). Hot bitumen, pumpable above 400 F and set by cooling, was injected with LMG and HMG; HMG wells were 10 ft upstream of the bitumen wells; delivery lines must be kept hot (pp. 8-54 to 8-56; Figure 8-15). Case History 3 (Walz et al. 2003): a sudden inflow over 35,000 gal/min into a dolomitic limestone quarry less than 1,500 ft from a river; the goal was 8,000 gal/min total inflow, requiring river inflow below 3,000 gal/min. An intercepting cutoff about 50 ft from the riverbank was built in nine phases: 'cold karst' with LMG and slurry through multiple packer sleeve pipes (MPSP), then 'hot karst' with hot bitumen from the downstream row backed by upstream slurry; river flow into the quarry essentially stopped (pp. 8-56 to 8-58). Case History 4 (Greenwood and Hill 2012): subsidence of 12 to 39 in. over areas up to 300 ft across; an LMG barrier (slump 2 to 4 in., holes at 10 to 20 ft) around the perimeter, HMG infill inside, strength above the 500 psi overburden, cutoff pressure 21 psi at the gage, plus LMG support columns (Figure 8-16) (pp. 8-58 to 8-59).
key_points: Case 1: holes 5 ft apart in three rows; foamed grout (60:40) saved 20-25%, 290 psi vs about 4000 psi
Case 2: hot bitumen (pumpable above 400 F) sealed a 35,000 gal/min conduit inflow with LMG/HMG
Case 3: cold karst grouted with LMG/MPSP first, then hot karst with bitumen backed by slurry
Case 4: LMG barrier slump 2-4 in., holes 10-20 ft; HMG infill; cutoff pressure 21 psi
