sections.title: Slabjacking
sections.summary: Slabjacking (slab stabilization) restores base/subgrade support to concrete pavement slabs by filling underlying voids with foam or grout; voids form at joints, cracks or edges from pumping or subgrade consolidation under repeated heavy loads (Fung and Smith 2010). Sensitive to construction practice, e.g., accidentally sealing transverse joints.
sections.body: Slabjacking, or slab stabilization, is a grouting technique used to restore base/subgrade support to concrete pavement slabs by filling the underlying voids with foam or grout. Voids develop beneath the slab at joints, cracks or the pavement edge due to pumping or consolidation of the subgrade caused by repetitive heavy traffic loads (Fung and Smith 2010). Slabjacking is sensitive to construction practices, and care should be taken when injecting foam or grout so as not to cause other problems, such as accidentally sealing the transverse joints (p. 8-59).
key_points: Fills voids under concrete slabs with grout or foam to restore support
Voids form at joints, cracks and edges from pumping or subgrade consolidation (Fung and Smith 2010)
Care needed not to seal transverse joints
sections.applicability: Restoring support to and re-leveling concrete pavement slabs.

sections.title: Applications
sections.summary: Slabjacking corrects settlement of slabs over consolidated organic soils, clays and silts or eroded materials, especially in highway maintenance: raising or leveling, under-slab void filling, joint grouting, asphalt subsealing. Mostly cementitious grouts with bentonite, sand, ash or fillers; proprietary expanding foams; best when uniform and gradual. A 1977 survey of state practices is quoted.
sections.body: Slabjacking is used to correct settlement of concrete slabs formed over soils such as organic soils, compressive clays and silts that have consolidated, or materials that have been washed or eroded away. It is especially appropriate for highway maintenance and preservation (Welsh 1997). Procedures include raising or leveling, under-slab void filling (no raising), grouting slab joints, and asphalt subsealing. Most slabjacking uses a suite of cementitious grouts incorporating bentonite, sand, ash and/or other fillers as dictated by local preference and project conditions and goals; certain proprietary methods use expanding chemical foams to create uplift pressures. Best results (no cracking of the slabs) are obtained when slabjacking is uniform and gradual. It can also be used to 'pump' expansion joints that have sunk below the adjoining section. A 1977 state-of-the-art study (Committee on Grouting of the Geotechnical Engineering Division 1977) summarized state transportation agency practice: slabjacking (raising or leveling), 25 states; under-slab void filling, 17 states; grouting slab joints, 6 states; subsealing (hot asphalt), 3 states; filling voids prior to overlay, 6 states (p. 8-60).
key_points: Corrects settlement of slabs over consolidated or eroded subgrades
Procedures: raising/leveling, under-slab void filling, joint grouting, asphalt subsealing
Mostly cementitious grouts with fillers; proprietary expanding foams also used
Best results when lifting is uniform and gradual
1977 survey: slabjacking 25 states, void filling 17, joint grouting 6, subsealing 3, pre-overlay void filling 6
sections.applicability: Highway maintenance uses of slabjacking.

sections.title: Advantages and Potential Disadvantages
sections.summary: Slabjacking advantages: often the most economical and fastest repair, little disruption, remote equipment, increased load capacity, longer service life from reduced deflections, smoother ride; most effective with minimal structural damage. Disadvantages: existing cracks may open, may not be cost-effective on small jobs, may not address the cause, not effective on badly distressed pavement.
sections.body: Advantages (2.6.2.1): slabjacking is frequently the most economical repair method; it is usually faster than other solutions, especially removal and replacement; it can be planned with little disruption to the existing facility and done at times of light or no traffic; the equipment can be remote from the repair location for maximum accessibility; increased load capacity of the slab is provided; the service life of concrete pavement is extended by reducing deflections; a smoother riding surface is established; and it is most effective when the pavement has undergone minimal structural damage (pp. 8-60 to 8-61). Potential disadvantages (2.6.2.2): cracks already present may tend to open up when the slab is treated unless care is taken; slabjacking may not be cost-effective on small projects; it may not address the original cause of the settlement; and it is not very effective on pavements that have already undergone significant structural damage (distresses) (p. 8-61).
key_points: Often most economical and fastest repair; little traffic disruption
Increases slab load capacity and service life by reducing deflections; smoother ride
Most effective when pavement has minimal structural damage
Existing cracks may open; may not address the cause of settlement
May not be cost-effective on small projects or effective on badly distressed pavement
sections.applicability: Deciding whether slabjacking suits a settled pavement or slab.

sections.title: Feasibility Evaluations
sections.summary: Feasibility of slabjacking rests on a cost analysis of replacing the slab and correcting the cause versus jacking it back and repeating periodically; slabjacking is typically not appropriate where cracking is severe; local contractors can supply budget estimates and feasibility studies.
sections.body: When a slab or structure has settled differentially, a cost analysis is key in determining whether to replace the slab and correct the cause of the problem, or to jack the slab back to its original elevation and repeat this process periodically. Slabjacking is typically not appropriate where the cracking is severe. Local contractors can be contacted to provide budget estimates and feasibility studies (p. 8-61).
key_points: Compare cost of replacing the slab and fixing the cause vs. periodic slabjacking
Not appropriate where cracking is severe
Local contractors can give budget estimates and feasibility studies

sections.title: Design Overview
sections.summary: Slabjacking design: grout of Portland cement, fine sand and water (5-10% cement gives strength over 480 Pa as printed), sand 100% passing #8 with not more than 20% finer than 0.002 in., accelerators, pozzolan 15-50% of cement weight for pumpability; define cause, end result and tolerances; injection holes on a 5-6 ft grid; monitor lift with string line or lasers.
sections.body: Grout types and selection (2.6.4.1): most slabjacking can be done with Portland cement, fine sand and water, with bentonite and chemical admixtures for rheology. Cement content of 5% to 10%, depending on sand gradation and admixtures, will be sufficient to provide a grout strength in excess of 480 Pa (as printed); higher cement gives higher strength. Water is adjusted for consistency. Sand should ideally be well graded, 100% passing a #8 (2.36-mm) sieve, with not more than 20% finer than 0.002 inches. Calcium chloride or high early strength cement accelerates set, and shrinkage or expansion control admixtures can be added. Where exceptionally high strengths or excessively coarse sands are involved, admixtures are generally not used, and pozzolan (15 to 50% of the cement weight) improves pumpability (pp. 8-61 to 8-62). Design procedure (2.6.4.2): the underlying cause and desired end result must be determined first; re-leveling of settlement may need future leveling, and a pavement to be overlaid may need virtually no lifting; the engineer should specify performance requirements and tolerances. Existing cracks will remain visible, and restored slabs will contain patched injection holes usually on a grid of 5 to 6 ft, so surface finish should be considered in advance. Performance monitoring (2.6.4.3): the objectives are to fill voids and raise the slab to about its original elevation without further damage; a string line can verify this, while lasers monitor more accurately (p. 8-62).
key_points: Grout: Portland cement, fine sand, water; 5-10% cement (strength printed as in excess of 480 Pa)
Sand 100% passing #8 (2.36 mm), not more than 20% finer than 0.002 in. (p. 8-61)
Pozzolan 15-50% of cement weight improves pumpability (p. 8-62)
Determine cause and end result; specify performance requirements and tolerances
Injection holes usually on a 5-6 ft grid
Monitor lift with a string line or, more accurately, lasers
sections.applicability: Mix design, layout and monitoring for slabjacking.

sections.title: Cost Data
sections.summary: Slabjacking unit cost exceeds plain under-slab void filling because of the care in raising a slab; for estimating, $300 per cubic yard of grout injected is a starting point; polyurethane slabjacking $70-$100 per square yard of slab raised up to 2 in.
sections.body: Because of the extra effort involved in delicately raising a slab, the unit cost is normally higher than for only filling voids beneath slabs. For estimating purposes, a cost of $300 per cubic yard of grout injected is a good starting point. Slabjacking using polyurethane may be estimated at $70 to $100 per square yard of slab raised up to 2 inches (p. 8-62).
key_points: Raising costs more than void filling alone
Estimating start point: $300 per cu yd of grout injected
Polyurethane: $70-$100 per sq yd of slab raised up to 2 in.
sections.applicability: Order-of-magnitude cost of slabjacking.

sections.title: Case Histories
sections.summary: Three slabjacking case histories: (1) trial cementitious grouting under airport rigid pavement with pressure control, LVDT, GPR and FWD evaluation (Ni and Cheng 2012); (2) injected high-density polyurethane lifting a bridge end panel and slab (Soltesz 2002); (3) a state DOT study of polyurethane slab jacking of bridge approach slabs over five years (Abu and Labarca 2007).
sections.body: Case History 1 (Ni and Cheng 2012): trial grouting under PCC airport slabs used a mix with w/c 0.8 and a 7% additive by cement weight; a circulating injection system kept the pressure increment over initial contact pressure below 7.1 psi to prevent uncontrolled heave; slabs were monitored with LVDTs on reference beams, voids found by GPR, and FWD tests on four slabs showed lower deflections (Figure 8-17). Grout volume exceeded slab area times the 0.04 in. maximum allowed heave, attributed to thick voids or permeation of the subbase (pp. 8-63 to 8-64). Case History 2 (Soltesz 2002): a two-component high-density polyurethane (polyhydroxy compound with catalysts and water, plus an isocyanate) was injected through 0.63-in. holes to lift a slab 3.5 to 4 in.; advantages are fast set (up to 90% of strength within 15 minutes), high strength, fewer smaller holes, light weight and low water infiltration. Six 20-in.-deep holes, then holes at 4 ft spacing to fill voids; 10.5 hours, $9.10 per lb, $42,260 for 4649 lb. Settlement after 24 months was 0.08 to 0.4 in., mostly in the first three months; samples gave 47.5 psi (low density) and 97.3 psi (high density) (pp. 8-64 to 8-65). Case History 3 (Abu and Labarca 2007): polyurethane injected through 5/8-in. holes under bridge approach slabs at two interstate and highway sites; quantities were 3,240 lb versus a 600 lb estimate (Figure 8-18) and 1,043 lb versus 550 lb, showing the need for GPR before lifting. Costs ($243 and $117 per sq yd) were below slab replacement ($425 per sq yd) but above HMA overlay ($45 and $63) and mudjacking. Foam injection was judged practical for differential settlement but not economical for filling voids (pp. 8-65 to 8-67).

Case 3: polyurethane quantities 2 to 5 times estimates; GPR recommended before lifting

sections.title: Jet Grouting
sections.summary: Jet grouting uses high-pressure, high-velocity erosive jets of water and/or air to break down soil, remove part of it and mix and replace it with cement grout, forming 'soilcrete' columns of engineered shape, size and properties; usable in almost any soil from gravels to sensitive clays. Three systems: one-fluid, two-fluid (grout in air cone) and three-fluid (water in air, then grout).
sections.body: The jet grouting technique employs high pressure, high velocity erosive jets of water and/or air to break down the soil structure, removing varying proportions of soil and mixing and replacing them with a cement-based grout. Soil particles not removed are mixed with the grout in situ to form a treated mass. Jet grouting is compatible with almost any soil type, from sands and gravels to highly sensitive clays (p. 8-67). It transforms soils into a mixture of soil and cement, 'soilcrete,' and permits the shape, size and properties of the treated masses, usually circular columns, to be engineered in advance with increasing precision (Figure 8-19); column design still depends on the soil properties. Cement grout is injected at high velocity at the base of the drill string; as the string is withdrawn and rotated slowly, the jet cuts and mixes the soil for a finite distance around it, forming column elements, and the erosive action can be enhanced by simultaneous high-pressure air and/or water (pp. 8-67 to 8-68). There are three distinct types (Figure 8-20; Bruce 1994, Wheeler and Burke 2000): One-Fluid System, in which the high-pressure grout jet simultaneously erodes and injects and the soil is only partially replaced; Two-Fluid System, a high-pressure cement jet inside a compressed air cone, giving a larger column than one-fluid and a higher degree of replacement, though often lower strength than three-fluid; and Three-Fluid System, an upper high-pressure water jet inside a compressed air envelope excavates and a lower jet (usually at lower pressure) emits grout to replace the slurried soil, typically with the highest degree of replacement (p. 8-68). Table 8-1 (Section 2.2.2) compares the systems.
key_points: Erosive jets of grout, water and/or air break down soil and mix/replace it with cement grout (soilcrete)

sections.title: Applications
sections.summary: Jet grouting applications: water control (horizontal and vertical, static water, contaminated soils with precautions), settlement control, underpinning (since 1986 in the U.S.; doubles as excavation support), scour protection, excavation support (including pre-placed cross bracing and reinforcement), liquefaction mitigation (cemented mass or cellular structure), karst treatment, and remedial treatment of gaps in retaining walls.
sections.body: Water control (2.7.1.1): effective in horizontal and vertical water control under static water conditions, since the grouted mass is generally less permeable and stronger than the in-situ soil; usable in contaminated soils with precautions for cleaning equipment, protecting personnel and disposing of spoils. Settlement control (2.7.1.2): provides foundation support through weak soft soils to competent strata by increasing the strength of the weaker soils. Underpinning (2.7.1.3): a viable alternative to conventional underpinning since its U.S. introduction in 1986; serving as both underpinning and excavation support it can have a considerable economic advantage; it is comparatively safe, since personnel never work beneath the structure and no load transfer connection to the existing foundation is needed. Scour protection (2.7.1.4): effective around bridge piers and marine works. Excavation support (2.7.1.5): can be done immediately next to and through adjacent footings, giving a vibration-less, safe and designable support; can place cross bracing before excavation to prevent inward deflection; steel reinforcement can be placed in the soilcrete for axial and lateral capacity (p. 8-69). Liquefaction mitigation (2.7.1.6): transforms liquefiable soil into a cemented mass or creates a cellular or honeycomb structure to stiffen it. Treatment of karst (2.7.1.7): used to remove clay from karstic features and replace it with engineered grout (Bruce 2003). Remedial treatments, gaps in retaining walls (2.7.1.8): columns used to improve strength or reduce permeability of soils at retaining walls (pp. 8-69 to 8-70).

sections.title: Feasibility Evaluations
sections.summary: Jet grouting treats clays to gravel, best in cohesionless or soft cohesive soils, above or below the water table, to depths over 150 ft (commonly under 100 ft). Not recommended in highly plastic soils or fibrous peat without pre-cutting; open-graded soils lose grout. Organics, low pH or flowing groundwater affect quality; CO2 emissions reduced; suited to congested, variable sites needing strength over 435 psi.
sections.body: Geotechnical (2.7.2.1): jet grouting can treat soils ranging from clays to gravel, with best results in cohesionless or soft cohesive soils. It can be performed above or below the groundwater table and has been installed to depths greater than 150 ft, although common applications are less than 100 ft deep. Its use in highly plastic soils and fibrous peat, which are less erodible, is not recommended unless particular action is taken, such as pre-cutting with water only. Very coarse or open-graded soils let the grout travel considerable distances and leave the zone to be treated. Soilcrete strength reflects the cement added and the initial soil type and consistency: sands and gravels give higher strength and more homogeneous soilcrete than silts and clays. Environmental (2.7.2.2): soilcrete quality is affected by organics, very low pH or flowing groundwater (Burke 2012). Efficiency gains have reduced carbon dioxide emissions from about 3.75 lb/cu ft (60 kg/m3) for triple-fluid jet grouting to less than 0.63 lb/cu ft (10 kg/m3) (Yoshida 2010). Jet grouting produces spoil, which can be re-used in earthworks (Pinto et al. 2012). Project conditions (2.7.2.3): jet grouting is particularly well suited to areas with a high density of structures or utilities, very variable ground, ground not amenable to other grouting techniques, and where significant strength (say over 435 psi) is required from the treated mass (p. 8-70).

Not recommended in highly plastic soils or fibrous peat unless pre-cut with water

sections.title: Design Considerations
sections.summary: Jet grouting design: 3- to 5-ft columns for underpinning and excavation support, sequenced for no more than 3 ft of temporary bridging; single-fluid soilcrete UCS guide (Table 8-6): sands/gravels 750-1,250 psi, silts/silty sands 500-750, clays 250-500, organics/peat < 250; strength rises with cement content; field test required; design values <= 50% of ultimate strength; columns 2.5-15 ft; w/c 0.8-1.2.
sections.body: When jet grouting is used for underpinning and excavation support, three- to five-foot-diameter columns are typically designed, sequenced so that no more than three feet of temporary bridging is required from the existing foundation. The single-fluid soilcrete strengths of Table 8-6 (Burke 2004) can guide feasibility: clean sands and gravel 750 to 1,250 psi; silts and silty sands 500 to 750 psi; clays 250 to 500 psi; organic silts and peats less than 250 psi (p. 8-71). Whatever the system, strength is a function of the cement content of the final product; the triple fluid system typically has higher replacement, hence more cement and higher strength; double-fluid strengths may be lower due to air entrainment. Acceptance requires at least a minimum number of jet grout samples to exceed a minimum 28-day unconfined compressive strength, both set by the engineer (ASCE 2009). Excavation support and underpinning should be designed by standard procedures for the loads transferred through the underpinned foundation. Because final strength depends on the in-situ soil and the contractor's equipment, means and methods, a production field test is essential to confirm column size, shape, verticality, homogeneity and strength. Design values should be restricted to 50% or less of the ultimate strength values (fc) to accommodate soilcrete variability (p. 8-71). Spacing (2.7.3.1): columns can be 2.5 to 15 ft in diameter depending on method, and can be overlapped in continuous rows in a primary/secondary sequence. Grout quantities (2.7.3.2): less dependent on soil than other grouting; they reflect the design requirement, e.g., load and achievable bearing capacity. Grout types (2.7.3.3): Portland cement with w/c 0.8 to 1.2, as low as 0.5 in three-fluid work; bentonite and additives relatively rare; slag cements of typically 50% slag and 50% Portland cement increasingly used (pp. 8-71 to 8-72).

sections.title: Cost
sections.summary: Jet grouting cost varies with complexity and depth: about $150 per cu yd on a complex clay project (1994); typically $115-$230 per cu yd. Table 8-7 gives prices per yard of depth for 3.0-3.6 ft columns (underpinning/excavation support $95-$550 unlimited headroom, $490-$650 restricted; seepage control $30-$115 and $30-$200); Table 8-8 gives 2004-2008 unit prices (mobilization $25,000-$150,000; jet grouting $100-$750 per CY).
sections.body: Jet grouting is designed to solve problems normally untreatable by other ground modification methods, and its cost varies greatly with project complexity and treatment depth. Costs on a complex project in clay were approximately $150 per cubic yard of ground treated (in 1994); the typical cost currently varies from $115 to $230 per cubic yard. Table 8-7 gives prices from more than 65 U.S. projects: for underpinning and excavation support with 3.0 to 3.6 ft diameter columns, per yard of depth, $95 to $550 with unlimited headroom (< 36 ft) and $490 to $650 with restricted headroom (10 to 13 ft); for seepage control, $30 to $115 and $30 to $200 respectively. These include mobilization, testing and demobilization of $25,000 to $50,000, typically 5% to 15% of overall cost. Jet grouting may also be measured as mobilization, demobilization and testing as a lump sum, or as a seepage barrier wall or underpinning measured per square yard (p. 8-72). Table 8-8 gives 2004-2008 unit prices: mobilization, 1 lump sum, $25,000 to $150,000 (rising beyond 500 miles; phased projects may need several mobilizations); jet grouting greater than 500 CY, $100 to $750 per CY, sensitive to the Portland cement content and far higher with headroom constraints. Payment is typically per cubic yard, including layout, spoil disposal and instrumentation, monitoring and QC, with mobilization paid separately. A pre-production test program is essential and must be paid for (p. 8-73).

sections.title: Case History
sections.summary: One jet grouting case history: reinforced jet-grouted soil-cement columns stabilizing a steep (to 1.1:1) 58.5-ft-deep highway ramp cut in faulted carbonate rock, raising the factor of safety from 1.2 to the required 1.5, with soil nails and a geocell face (Meyers et al. 2003).
sections.body: Case History 1 (Meyers et al. 2003): stabilization of excavation of deep cut sections using jet grouting for highway ramp construction. Design constraints required a very steep slope (1:1) to avoid encroaching on an adjacent historical property; the final section was cut to 58.5 ft deep, with slope varying from 2:1 to 1.1:1 to 2:1 within 105 ft, to meet the owner's requirement of a factor of safety of 1.5 for permanent slopes. Retaining wall configurations did not give feasible solutions. Reinforced soil-cement columns forming 'cut-off' walls were built by jet grouting, and the slope face was stabilized with a geocell product pinned by drilled soil anchors. The site was a highly faulted, folded and fractured carbonate formation (limestone and dolomite) prone to solution weathering and sinkholes. Slope stability analysis showed steel-pipe-reinforced jet grouted columns raised the factor of safety from 1.2 to the minimum 1.5. Columns 2.5 ft in diameter were placed in a zigzag pattern in two rows, one near the toe and one at one-third of the slope length from the toe (Figure 8-21); soil nails of 4-inch neat cement grout with 1-inch steel bars were built on a 15 ft x 15 ft grid over the slope (p. 8-74). Columns were built in three stages with a method installing column and reinforcement together. UCS tests gave acceptable values (approximately greater than 500 psi) when sulfur caps rather than neoprene caps were used. The final cost was $1,300,000 for the slope. Jet grouting was found effective, highly cost-effective and quicker than alternatives such as retaining walls (p. 8-75).

sections.title: Rock Fissure Grouting
sections.summary: Rock fissure grouting, used mostly in dam and tunnel construction and rehabilitation, provides low-permeability hydraulic cut-offs and can bind rock masses mechanically; also used to locate and seal major voids. Categories with particulate grouts: curtain grouting (two or more lines), area (blanket/consolidation) grouting, tunnel grouting (contact, ground treatment, pre-excavation), and backfilling of boreholes.
sections.body: Rock fissure grouting is most commonly used in dam and tunnel construction and rehabilitation for structural stability and groundwater control. It primarily provides hydraulic cut-off zones of relatively low permeability, but can also bind rock masses mechanically to enhance load-bearing properties, and can be applied wherever there is a hydraulic or structural need to fill fissures in rock. For transportation facilities, potential applications include shaft repair, remediation of deteriorating road or railway tunnels, and stabilization of rock slopes; it can also form remedial grout curtains to prevent sinkholes and depressions caused by dewatering and/or movement of fines in highways next to active quarries (p. 8-75). Similar drilling and grouting are used to locate and seal major voids in rock, natural (karstic limestone, salt solution cavities) or man-made (coal or iron mines), which can cause surface settlement or allow large water flows. Rock grouting with particulate materials normally falls into these categories: curtain grouting, the drilling and grouting of two or more lines of grout holes to produce a seepage barrier, usually extended into materials judged acceptably impermeable; area grouting (also 'blanket' or 'consolidation' grouting), a shallow zone grouted through holes in a pattern or grid to mechanically improve fractured and jointed rock, sometimes deeper in fault zones or at shafts and buried structures; tunnel grouting, to fill voids behind liners (contact grouting), treat surrounding material, or control seepage, including pre-excavation grouting from the surface or face; and backfilling of exploration boreholes and grout holes to maximize stability, control water or prevent passage of contaminants (p. 8-76).

sections.title: Applications
sections.summary: The most common use of rock grouting today is in dam and tunnel construction and rehabilitation, especially for structural stability and groundwater control (Weaver and Bruce 2007); transportation applications include shaft repair, remediation of deteriorating road or railway tunnels, and rock slope stabilization.
sections.body: As noted in the section introduction, the most common use of rock grouting today is in dam and tunnel construction and rehabilitation, especially for structural stability and groundwater control (Weaver and Bruce 2007). For transportation facilities, potential applications include shaft repair, the remediation of deteriorating road or railway tunnels, and the stabilization of rock slopes (p. 8-76).
key_points: Most common use: dam and tunnel construction and rehabilitation (Weaver and Bruce 2007)
Transportation: shaft repair, road/railway tunnel remediation, rock slope stabilization

sections.title: Advantages and Potential Disadvantages
sections.summary: Rock fissure grouting can repair weak or permeable rock where alternatives are costly removal or abandonment; it reduces permeability and deformability and increases shear strength (Lombardi 2003). Inefficiencies from poor design and practice: uplift from excessive pressure, premature plugging, wrong hole spacing or orientation, inappropriate verification; avoided by experienced personnel.
sections.body: Advantages (2.8.2.1): rock fissure grouting can repair weak or permeable rock masses where limited alternatives exist, ranging from costly removal and replacement to abandoning the site. The main advantages (Lombardi 2003) are reducing the permeability of the rock mass, reducing its deformability, and increasing its strength, particularly against shear forces (p. 8-77). Potential disadvantages (2.8.2.2): inefficiencies arise from poor design and poor field practice, including inducing uplift and damage to foundations from excessive pressures; premature plugging of fissures by thickening the mix too quickly, by unsuitable injection methods or formulations, or by inappropriate drilling and flushing techniques; improper spacing or orientation of grout holes; and inappropriate verification. These can be rectified by knowledgeable and experienced personnel designing, constructing, supervising, inspecting and controlling the drilling and grouting operations (p. 8-77).
key_points: Reduces rock mass permeability and deformability; increases shear strength (Lombardi 2003)
Risk: uplift and foundation damage from excessive pressure
Risk: premature plugging from thickening too quickly or poor drilling/flushing

sections.title: Feasibility Evaluations
sections.summary: Rock grouting feasibility: groutability ratio NR = width of fissure / (D95)grout (Eq. 8-6); grouting consistently possible for NR > 5, not possible for NR < 2, and grout fineness and rheology should be engineered so the feasibility number is nearer 3 than 5. Measure in-situ permeability (Lugeon tests, 1 Lu = 0.5 x 10^-6 in/s), staged up-and-down pressures; environmental risk to water bodies; thorough investigation and design-phase test program.
sections.body: Geotechnical (2.8.3.1): the main consideration in grouting rock fissures, for water control or structural improvement, is the grain size of the particulate grout compared with the width of the fracture. The groutability ratio NR for rock fissures is given by Eq. 8-6, where D is the grout diameter and the subscript is the percent finer (Mitchell 1981). As rock characteristics cannot be changed, the fineness of the grout should be controlled and its rheology engineered so that the NR number for rock grouting feasibility is nearer 3 than 5, with: NR > 5, grouting consistently possible; NR < 2, grouting not possible (pp. 8-77 to 8-78). In-situ permeability must be measured in advance since it governs design, construction and verification; rock mass stability is also vital. The Lugeon value is convenient for grout curtain design (Weaver and Bruce 2007) and is printed as equal to 0.11 inch^2/psi (1 L/m/bar) at a test pressure of 145 psi (10 bar); 1 Lugeon (Lu) = 0.5 x 10^-6 inches/second (1.3 x 10^-5 cm/s). Testing at different pressures in an up-and-down order (low-moderate-high-moderate-low) helps study the elasticity of fissure openings, grout flow, voids (Houlsby 1990, Weaver and Bruce 2007) and hydrofracture (Littlejohn 1992) (p. 8-78). Environmental (2.8.3.2): grout leaking into a body of water may deplete oxygen or change pH and cause a fish kill. Project conditions (2.8.3.3): a thorough investigation is needed since rock may be weak, fractured, voided, highly permeable, erodible or soluble; in situ permeability (Lugeon) testing and an optical televiewer are essential; a design-phase test program is often warranted to develop the final design and cost estimate, tied to the local geology (p. 8-78).

sections.title: Limitations
sections.summary: Rock grouting costs are hard to pre-assess: complex, variable site geology means even test program statistics may not fix costs reliably; recent grout curtains in carbonate terrains have cost between $25 and $80 per sq. ft of curtain (as printed here; Section 2.8.6.2 gives $25 to $80 per square yard).
sections.body: Experience has shown that it can be difficult to pre-assess the cost of a rock grouting program. Site geology can be extremely complex, with widely differing subsurface conditions within the site boundaries. Even when a test program is performed, its statistical results may still not be sufficient to determine project costs with a reliable degree of accuracy, and these factors prevent accurate cost estimation of rock grouting operations. However, recent grout curtains in carbonate terrains have cost between $25 and $80 per sq. feet of curtain (p. 8-79). Note that the general guide in Section 2.8.6.2 (p. 8-85) prints the same range per square yard of curtain.

sections.title: Design Considerations
sections.summary: Rock grouting design: extent, rows, materials, hole spacing/inclination/diameter, quantities, methods, performance and verification, monitoring and contract documents, with a clearly stated goal (residual permeability or strength). Balanced multi-component particulate grouts; water flush, pressure washing and testing; pressure rules of thumb 1 to 4 times overburden weight (Figure 8-22); upstage, downstage and MPSP methods (Table 8-9); real-time computer monitoring mandatory.
sections.body: Design defines extent, rows, materials, hole spacing, inclination and diameter, quantities, methods, verification, monitoring and contract documents. The goal must be clearly stated, e.g., a specific residual permeability by post-grouting tests, or increased strength or homogeneity by core testing, load testing or cross-hole seismic methods (p. 8-79). Grout types (2.8.5.1): primarily particulate; traditional practice was incorrectly based on neat cement, while current practice uses balanced multi-component formulations with controlled fluid and set properties (ASCE 2003; Weaver and Bruce 2007). Design procedure (2.8.5.2): record discontinuity frequency and aperture and in-situ permeability; water flush is essential for fissure grouting; holes are flushed, pressure washed and pressure tested immediately before grouting, at pressures not exceeding, and used to set, the maximum allowable grouting pressure. Rules of thumb for grouting pressure range from 1 to 4 times the theoretical weight of rock above the injection point (Figure 8-22); the maximum safe pressure must be confirmed by preconstruction testing (pp. 8-79 to 8-80). Methods for stable rock are upstage, downstage with top-hole packer, and downstage with down-hole packer (Figure 8-23; Table 8-9). Downstage consolidates from the top down and adapts depth and stage length but needs rig moves and redrilling; upstage drills in one pass and is cheaper but has a predetermined depth and risks collapse and upward grout escape. Competent dam rock suits upstage, historically most common; the top stage is often downstaged; in extremely weathered or collapsing ground the multiple packer sleeve pipe (MPSP, Figure 8-24) is preferred (Bruce and Gallavresi 1988) (pp. 8-81 to 8-83). Performance monitoring (2.8.5.3): real-time computer monitoring/recording should always be mandatory (Bruce 2012); computerized monitoring is now standard practice, and performance must also be monitored in service (pp. 8-83 to 8-84).

sections.title: Cost Data
sections.summary: Rock grouting bidding: separate pay items per work aspect; quantities vary, so contracts allow changes without changing unit prices; drilling paid per linear foot (redrilling set grout typically 50% of rock drilling rate), pressure testing and washing hourly, materials by weight, injection per pump hour. Estimates from test grouting, borings, experience and unit takes; a grout curtain may cost $25 to $80 per square yard.
sections.body: Bidding methods (2.8.6.1): rock grouting may be part of a general contract or a separate contract. As for all grouting, pay items for individual aspects of the work are listed separately, the approach of choice of government agencies. Routine instrumentation is typically included in other items. Because of uncertainty, accurate quantity estimates are extremely difficult, and contracts often reserve the right to increase or eliminate any part of the program without changing unit prices. Grout and exploratory hole drilling are paid per linear foot drilled, usually including washing; pressure testing and washing are separate hourly items; redrilling set grout is typically priced at 50% of the rock drilling rate; materials are paid by weight of each component injected; and grout injection by the pump hour (p. 8-84). Cost estimation methods (2.8.6.2): quantities can only be approximated; specifications and bid items should let estimated quantities vary substantially without affecting unit prices, but a concerted effort must still be made to estimate drilling and grout take, using pre-construction test grouting, boring evaluations, experience and unit-take estimates. Drawings and specifications should give hole spacing, sequencing, direction, maximum angle and depth, and allowable deviation. Additional items: drilling exploratory and verification holes (per linear foot), drilling drain holes (separate items by size and location), and instrumentation (monitoring may be separate). Input should be sought from agencies and specialty contractors. As a general guide, a grout curtain may cost $25 to $80 per square yard of curtain, including all drilling, grouting and materials (pp. 8-84 to 8-85).

sections.title: Case Histories
sections.summary: Two rock grouting case histories: (1) computer monitoring and analysis of grout curtains at three dams, with monitoring Levels 1-3 (dipstick and gage; real-time data collection; advanced integrated analytical systems) (Dreese et al. 2003); (2) multi-phase grouting of a karstic limestone dam foundation from 1942 to 2011, with balanced stable grouts, computer control and Lugeon closure criteria (Bruce et al. 2014).
sections.body: Case History 1 (Dreese et al. 2003): computer monitoring and real-time analysis give more data, higher grouting pressures, faster and more consistent operations and better use of resources; plots of Lugeon value, or flow divided by effective pressure, against time flag problems such as unsafe pressures. Level 1, dipstick and gage, used before 2000, readings every 5 to 15 minutes plotted by hand; Level 2, real-time electronic collection, display and storage; Level 3, advanced integrated analytical systems combining data, display, query and CAD. Level 3 is recommended for projects over $750,000 and Level 2 for projects over $250,000 (p. 8-86). At one dam about 180 ft high and 2,000 ft long, a triple-row curtain used neat grout with Level 1 on the first row and balanced, stable modified grouts with Level 2 on the others (lower cohesion, bleed and pressure filtration, strength above 200 psi); quality improved at reduced cost (Figures 8-25, 8-26). A limestone ridge seepage project used stable grouts and Level 2 monitoring, cut permeability by up to three orders of magnitude, with residual about 1 Lugeon (Figures 8-27, 8-28). At a third dam, a single-line curtain 1100 ft long to 120 ft deep met a 5-Lugeon criterion; 3D displays located an unexpected permeable dike (Figures 8-29, 8-30) (pp. 8-87 to 8-93). Case History 2 (Bruce et al. 2014): a 5,736-ft-long dam up to 258 ft high on karstic limestone developed sinkholes and muddy flow in 1968. Phase 1 (1942-43): 600 downstage holes, neat grout w/c 0.66, holes on 10-ft centers about 50 ft deep. Phase 2 (1968-75): emergency holes 6.75 in. at 2.5 ft centers grouted by gravity, then 852 holes and two concrete diaphragm walls (1975-79). Phase 3 (2007-08): two-line curtain 3,840 ft long with balanced stable grout, targets 10 Lugeons in the wall zone and 3 Lugeons below it. Phase 4 (2009-11): LMG and HMG, about 274,000 linear ft drilled and 375,000 gallons injected (Figures 8-31 to 8-33) (pp. 8-93 to 8-96).

sections.summary: Introduces Section 3 on the general grouting equipment and materials used on grouting projects: rock and soil drilling methods, grouting plant, and the four categories of grout materials.
sections.body: This section addresses general grouting equipment and materials used on grouting projects (p. 8-97). Section 3.1 covers construction equipment: the three types of rock drilling, measurement while drilling, soil drilling methods and grouting equipment. Section 3.2 covers materials: particulate grouts, colloidal solutions, pure solutions (resins) and miscellaneous grouts.

Section 3.2: grout materials in four categories

sections.title: Construction Equipment
sections.summary: Equipment used for grouting and for rock and soil drilling; the three types of rock drilling are high rotation speed/low torque rotary, low rotation speed/high torque rotary, and rotary percussive.
sections.body: This section discusses equipment used for grouting and for rock and soil drilling. There are basically three types of rock drilling: 1) high rotation speed/low torque rotary drilling, 2) low rotation speed/high torque rotary drilling, and 3) rotary percussive drilling (p. 8-97). The subsections describe each drilling type, summarize drilling requirements and hole deviation limits, measurement while drilling, soil drilling methods, and grouting equipment (mixers, agitators, pumps and plant).
key_points: Three rock drilling types: high speed/low torque rotary, low speed/high torque rotary, rotary percussive
sections.applicability: Selecting drilling and grouting equipment for a grouting project.

sections.title: High Rotation Speed/Low Torque Rotary Drilling
sections.summary: High-speed, low-torque rotary drilling makes grout holes up to 3 in. diameter to depths of 160-800 ft with light rigs, coring or using blind diamond bits (Figure 8-34); slow and prone to deviation, it is now rarely used for production grout holes. Advantages include dual use for investigation, continuous exploration, little fissure clogging, low vibration, smooth hole walls.
sections.body: High rotation speed, low torque drilling is typically used for grout holes up to 3 inches in diameter to depths of 160 to 800 ft. Relatively light rigs can extract core samples with a core barrel system, or simply drill grout holes with 'blind' or 'plug' diamond impregnated bits (Figure 8-34). Because of slow penetration rates and deviation issues, such methods are rarely used nowadays for grout hole production drilling (p. 8-97). Advantages are: the same equipment can be used for investigation and grout hole drilling; continuous or intermittent exploration of the rock is possible over the whole hole; drilling can reach relatively great depths, though not typically required; no or limited clogging of rock fissures occurs, since cuttings are removed with the flush water; vibration is minimized, making it the preferred technique through existing masonry and brickwork; it can drill all kinds of rock; most power sources (air, electricity, diesel) can be used; rotary bits produce smooth hole walls that ease packer installation; and good penetration speeds are possible in soft formations (pp. 8-97 to 8-98).

Light rigs; core barrel or blind/plug diamond bits

sections.title: Low Rotation Speed/High Torque Rotary
sections.summary: Low-speed, high-torque rotary drilling uses heavier, more powerful rigs to drill larger-diameter holes to considerable depths; penetration also depends on the thrust on the bit. Carbide drilling tools are shown in Figure 8-35.
sections.body: Low rotation speed, high torque drilling is used with heavier and more powerful rigs to drill holes of greater diameter to considerable depths. The penetration rate also depends on the amount of thrust applied to the bit. A variety of carbide drilling tool bits are shown in Figure 8-35 (p. 8-98). It is the second of the three basic types of rock drilling listed in Section 3.1, between high-speed rotary and rotary percussive drilling.
key_points: Heavier, more powerful rigs for larger, deeper holes
Penetration rate depends on thrust applied to the bit

sections.title: Rotary Percussive
sections.summary: Rotary percussive drilling: top hammer (60-120 rpm, holes seldom above 4 in., depth about 200 ft) or down-the-hole hammer (10-60 rpm, 3.3 in. and above, over 330 ft). Holes for fissure grouting must be water flushed; air-powered down-the-hole drilling is not acceptable for fissure grouting, but water-powered hammers are. Higher, consistent penetration, lighter rigs, lower cost.
sections.body: Rotary percussive drilling uses bits that are both percussed and rotated (cross or button). Percussive energy governs penetration, either with a top hammer, where the rods are rotated and percussed by the drill head, or a down-the-hole hammer, where larger rods are only rotated and compressed air or high-pressure water drives a hammer above the bit. Top hammer drilling runs at about 60 to 120 rpm in holes seldom above 4 inches, with grout hole depth limited to about 200 ft by power and deviation. Down-the-hole drilling runs at about 10 to 60 rpm in holes of 3.3 inches and above to depths over 330 ft. Percussion-drilled grout holes should be water flushed to avoid cuttings clogging fissures; below the water table, air flushing is risky as sludge may seal fissures, so air-powered down-the-hole drilling is not acceptable for fissure grouting, although water-powered hammers keep the speed and straightness benefits (Bruce et al. 2013). Advantages: higher and more consistent penetration in rock, smaller and lighter rigs, lower cost than rotary, and adaptability to layers of different hardness (p. 8-99). Top hammer is most common and cheapest but limits depth and has the greatest deviation, meaning more holes, more cost and lower quality; down-the-hole gives straighter, deeper holes. The choice should relate to geology, hole depth and diameter. U.S. rock drilling is traditionally rotary, but top drive rotary percussion with water or foam flush is growing; air flush is applicable to locate and fill large voids such as karst, and water-powered down-the-hole hammers offer cost and technical advantages for fissure drilling (pp. 8-99 to 8-100).

Down-the-hole: 10-60 rpm, holes 3.3 in. and above, depths over 330 ft

sections.title: Rock Drilling Summary
sections.summary: Drilling method must drill a straight hole, keep walls from caving, produce flushable cuttings that do not close fissures, and be cost-effective; holes should intercept as many fissures as possible (at least two rows inclined left and right). Attainable deviations: high-speed rotary 2-5% to 260 ft; top hammer long holes 15-20% (under 5% with guide rods), shallow to 40-50 ft under 5%; down-the-hole under 2% (under 1% with good workmanship).
sections.body: The drilling method selected must drill a straight hole; protect the hole walls from caving; produce cuttings small enough to flush out without closing fissures or blocking later grouting; and be cost-effective. Grout holes should intercept as many fissures as possible; where that is hard, spacing must be reduced so unfavorably oriented fissures are still grouted, so there are always at least two rows of holes inclined to the left and right. Larger cores give more reliable information, and larger holes are straighter but more expensive; packers are costlier and harder to set and backfilling costs more. Excessive deviation may leave unpenetrated 'windows' in a curtain; for deep holes, guide rods (centralizers), drill string supports and thicker rods may be used (p. 8-100). Commonly attainable deviation limits: high speed rotary drilling, normally 2 to 5% to depths of 260 ft; top hammer drilling, long holes 15 to 20% (under 5% with guide rods, with high risk of sticking), shallow holes down to 40 to 50 ft under 5% even without guide rods; down-the-hole drilling, typically less than 2%, and less than 1% with high standards of workmanship. Cuttings vary from muddy clay to flaky gravel; all grout holes must be cleaned of cuttings and loose material in the cracks, generally by high-pressure water flushing from the bottom up toward the collar (Weaver and Bruce 2007) (pp. 8-100 to 8-101).
key_points: Requirements: straight hole, stable walls, flushable cuttings, cost-effective
At least two rows of holes inclined left and right to intercept fissures
Deviation: high-speed rotary 2-5% to 260 ft; top hammer long holes 15-20% (under 5% with guide rods)
Down-the-hole: typically < 2%, < 1% with high workmanship (p. 8-101)
Excess deviation leaves unpenetrated windows in a curtain

sections.title: Measurement While Drilling (MWD)
sections.summary: MWD continuously records drilling parameters (depth, rate of penetration, weight on bit, feed force, rpm, torque, flush water flow and pressure, time) on percussive or rotary rigs to categorize the ground; correlate with nearby core. A pressure drop with flow increase locates fissures. It complements but does not replace manual logging.
sections.body: MWD is a method for continuous recording of drilling parameters. It measures the rig's behavior during drilling and gives a broad categorization of the ground. Measured variables can be depth, rate of penetration (ROP), weight on bit (WOB), feed force, rpm, torque, flush water flow, flush water pressure and time; MWD is usable on both percussive and rotary rigs. Recorded parameters vary with the ground, mainly hydraulic flow, pressure and penetration rate, but different geological conditions can give similar hydraulic characteristics, so the parameters should be correlated with drilled core from a nearby hole. Feed force and rpm are set by the driller; ROP and torque depend on the formation; flush water flow and pressure depend on driller, equipment and formation. The relation of flush water flow to pressure can locate major fissures and cracks: when the bit hits a fissure, pressure drops and flow increases as flush water flows into the fissure. The data may be electronic or manual and help in understanding the ground and the changes each phase of drilling and grouting makes. Automated MWD is increasingly common but does not completely replace normal manual logging; both data sets should be studied (p. 8-101).
key_points: Records depth, ROP, weight on bit, feed force, rpm, torque, flush flow and pressure, time
Usable on percussive and rotary rigs; correlate with nearby core

sections.title: Soil Drilling Methods
sections.summary: Many overburden drilling systems exist for soil grouting; choice should meet geometric needs and the soil's geotechnical and environmental challenges. Hollow stem augers, flushed casings, rotary duplex, percussive duplex and double-head duplex are used by region; flush choice is critical (never air in cohesionless soils below the water table); sonic drilling is fast and minimally disturbing.
sections.body: There is a wide range of overburden drilling systems for soil grouting. The choice should satisfy the geometric requirements and be consistent with the geotechnical and environmental challenges of the soil. The logic of choice is perhaps more obscure than in rock drilling, and history and habit mean not all methods are used by any one contractor or in any one region: hollow stem augers, simple flushed casings and rotary duplex are each favored in different regions, and rental companies have spread percussive duplex and double-head duplex nationwide. Percussive duplex (eccentric) is in general decline for routine production holes, though still regarded by some as the premier method in very difficult conditions, and has recently been replaced by a system using 'wings' to oversize the hole so the casing can be introduced with minimal torque. The choice of flush is critical, especially in cohesionless materials below the water table, where air should never be used. Sonic drilling has become very popular where minimal damage to surrounding soil is needed (e.g., through an existing embankment dam); it is fast, reliable and uses little or no flush (Bruce 2003) (p. 8-102).

sections.title: Grouting Equipment
sections.summary: Grouting equipment: mixer of adequate capacity, continuously agitated storage, pump with precise pressure and volume control, parameter recording, grout lines and header, packers, gauges and valves (Figure 8-36), now often computer controlled. High-shear colloidal mixers are far superior for HMG; bentonite fully pre-hydrated; piston or progressive cavity pumps for HMG, concrete pumps for LMG, custom equipment for chemical and jet grouting (Figures 8-37 to 8-47).
sections.body: Many types of grouting equipment are available, and each major grouting technique basically demands its own. The main components are grout mixing equipment of adequate capacity mixing to a uniform consistency; a storage tank with continuous agitation to prevent settlement and segregation; a pump with precise pressure and volume control; grout parameter recording equipment; and grout lines with a header for injecting into the hole; plus suitable packers, gauges, valves and accessories. A schematic layout for HMG injection is in Figure 8-36; much of this is now replaced with a sophisticated computer-controlled plant/pump operation (p. 8-102). Mixer and agitator need not have the same capacity; for high takes two mixers may feed one storage tank; both should agitate continuously until the grout is injected or wasted. For HMGs, high-speed, high-shear (colloidal) mixers are far superior to slow-speed mechanical mixers, producing more uniform, better grout more quickly. Bentonite is mixed separately and must be fully hydrated before entering the grout mixer. Water is metered into the mixers by a meter calibrated in liters; the metric system is numerically advantageous for batching. Piston or progressive cavity pumps are used for HMG, concrete pumps (modified as necessary) for LMG grouting, and custom-built equipment for chemical and jet grouting (p. 8-103). Typical drilling and grouting equipment is shown in Figures 8-37 to 8-47 (pp. 8-104 to 8-109).

sections.title: Materials
sections.summary: Grout materials fall into four categories in order of increasing rheological performance and cost (Bruce et al. 1997): (1) particulate (suspension, cementitious) grouts, Binghamian; (2) colloidal solutions, evolutive Newtonian; (3) pure solutions, non-evolutive Newtonian; (4) miscellaneous. Category 3 grouts can permeate silty sands (k = 4 x 10^-5 in/s). Table 8-10 compares water control grouts.
sections.body: Grouting materials can be classified into four categories, in order of increasing rheological performance and cost (Bruce et al. 1997): 1) particulate (suspension or cementitious) grouts, having Binghamian performance (Figure 8-48 left); 2) colloidal solutions, evolutive Newtonian fluids whose viscosity increases with time (Figure 8-48 right); 3) pure solutions, non-evolutive Newtonian solutions whose viscosity is essentially constant until setting, within an adjustable period; and 4) miscellaneous materials. Category 1 comprises water and one or more particulate solids such as cement, fly ash, clays or sand; mixes may be stable (minimal bleeding) or unstable at rest, and stable thixotropic grouts have cohesion and plastic viscosity increasing with time, accelerated under excess pressure (p. 8-109). Categories 2 and 3 are now commonly called solution or chemical grouts, subdivided by chemistry into silicate based (Category 2) or resins (Category 3); the rheology and low viscosity of certain Category 3 grouts permit permeation of soils as fine as silty sands (k = 4 x 10^-5 inch/second). Category 4 comprises relatively exotic materials, used infrequently but of growing importance, e.g., hot bitumen for fast flow sealing (Bruce 2003) (p. 8-110). Table 8-10 summarizes Category 2 and 3 water control grouts: silicates, low viscosity (> 6 cP), low toxicity, medium strength, > $0.13/quart, fine fissures; lignosulfites, medium (> 8 cP), high toxicity, low strength, > $0.26; polyurethane, high (> 400 cP), high toxicity, high strength, > $1.32, large fissures; acrylamides, low (1.2 cP), high toxicity, low strength, > $0.53, very fine fissures; acrylates, low (1.2 cP), low toxicity, low strength, > $0.53, very fine fissures (p. 8-111).

sections.title: Particulate Grouts
sections.summary: Particulate grouts are the most common for waterproofing and strengthening; water-to-solids ratio governs properties. Subcategories: neat cement, clay/bentonite-cement, with fillers, special applications, enhanced penetrability. w/c by volume = 1.5 x by weight. Portland cement Types I-V; microfine cements max particle < 8 microns, bulk < 4 microns (Figure 8-49). Pressure filtration coefficient Kpf and filter cake growth coefficient Kpc (Eq. 8-7).
sections.body: Because of their characteristics and relative economy, particulate grouts remain the most commonly used for routine waterproofing and ground strengthening. The water-to-solids ratio is a prime determinant of stability, fluidity, rheology, strength and durability. Subcategories: neat cement grouts; clay/bentonite-cement grouts; grouts with fillers; grouts for special applications; and grouts with enhanced penetrability. In the U.S. w/c ratios have been expressed by volume, but semi-automatic batching favors weight ratios; a grout with w/c = 1 by weight comprises approximately 12 gallons (100 liters) of water and 242.5 lb (100 kg) of cement; as a rule of thumb, w/c by volume = 1.5 x w/c by weight (pp. 8-111 to 8-112). Portland cements: Type I, general purpose; Type II, moderate sulfate resistance and slower heat of hydration; Type III, high early strength, used for quick service or emergency repairs and, being finer, sometimes for slightly finer fissures; Type IV, low heat, slow strength gain, for mass placements; Type V, severe sulfate exposure. Microfine cements are finer ground Portland or blast furnace slag cements, typically with maximum particle size less than 3.2 x 10^-4 in. (8 microns) and the bulk less than 1.6 x 10^-4 in. (4 microns) (Figure 8-49) (p. 8-112). Many particulate grouts are unsuited to high flow, high head conditions, being diluted or washed away before setting; low mobility grouts, in the third subgroup, can reduce seepage under suitable conditions. When grout is forced into a small aperture under pressure, water can be expelled and a cementitious filter cake forms that eventually blocks the aperture. This is quantified by the pressure filtration coefficient Kpf and the filter cake growth coefficient Kpc (Eq. 8-7; Weaver and Bruce 2007) (p. 8-113). A low pressure filtration coefficient, minimizing the rise in apparent viscosity, is required to increase penetrability; Figure 8-50 shows Kpf against cohesion (p. 8-114).

sections.title: Colloidal Solutions
sections.summary: Colloidal solutions are sodium silicate plus reagent, gelling with time; silicate characterized by molecular ratio Rp (typically 3-4) and density 30-42 degrees Baume; organic reagents give soft or hard gels, inorganic reagents give weak gels for waterproofing only. Sodium silicate grouts are unsuitable for permanent barriers under high flow/high head (set 20-60 min, strength < 290 psi, poor durability).
sections.body: Colloidal solutions comprise mixtures of sodium silicate and reagent solutions that change in viscosity over time to produce a gel. Sodium silicate is an alkaline, colloidal aqueous solution characterized by its molecular ratio, Rp, and specific density in degrees Baume; typically Rp is 3-4 and density 30-42 degrees Baume. Reagents may be organic or inorganic (mineral). Organic reagents cause a saponification reaction that frees acids and can give soft or hard gels depending on concentrations; common types include monoesters, diesters, triesters and aldehydes, while organic acids and esters are now much less common. Inorganic reagents, such as sodium bicarbonate and sodium aluminate, neutralize silicate alkalinity; to get a satisfactory hardening time the silicate must be strongly diluted, so these gels are weak and of use only for waterproofing (pp. 8-114 to 8-115). The proportions of silicate and reagent determine gel time, viscosity, strength, syneresis and durability, as well as cost and environmental acceptability. In general sodium silicate grouts are unsuitable for permanent seepage barriers against high-flow/high-head conditions because of relatively long setting time (20-60 minutes), low strength (less than 290 psi) and poor durability, though they may be acceptable for temporary use, say less than a few months. Sodium silicate without reagent may be used to accelerate stiffening of cementitious grouts against fast flows in small orifices (p. 8-115).

Typical Rp 3-4; density 30-42 degrees Baume (p. 8-114)
Inorganic-reagent gels are weak: waterproofing only
Not for permanent high-flow/high-head barriers: set 20-60 min, strength < 290 psi, poor durability (p. 8-115)

sections.title: Pure Solutions
sections.summary: Resins are organic solutions that gel by polymerization or polycondensation, with set time controlled by component proportions; used where very low viscosity, fast strength gain, variable set, chemical resistance or resistance to high flow are needed. Four types (Table 8-11): acrylic, phenolic, aminoplastic, polyurethane; water-reactive (hydrophobic or hydrophilic) and two-component polyurethanes are usually appropriate for grouting.
sections.body: Resins are solutions of organic products in water or a non-aqueous solvent that form a gel with specific mechanical properties under normal temperature in a closed environment. They react by polymerization, activated by a catalyst (e.g., poly-acrylamide resins), or by polymerization and polycondensation of two components (e.g., epoxies, aminoplasts); setting time is controlled by the proportions. Resins are used when particulate grouts or colloidal solutions are inadequate: for particularly low viscosity, very fast strength gain (a few hours), variable setting time (seconds to hours), superior chemical resistance, special (pseudoplastic) rheology, or resistance to high groundwater flows (pp. 8-115 to 8-116). They are used for strengthening and waterproofing where durability is essential. Four categories (Table 8-11): acrylic (granular very fine soils, finely fissured rock: mass waterproofing, gas tightening, strengthening up to 220 psi, granular media under vibration); phenol (very fine granular soils: strengthening); aminoplastic (schists and coals: strengthening by adherence to organic materials); polyurethane (large voids: foam barrier against running water with water-reactive resins, stabilization or localized filling with two-component resins). Chrome lignosulfonates are not discussed because of their toxic components. Only two polyurethane groups are usually appropriate: water-reactive polyurethanes, which react with groundwater to give flexible or rigid foam, viscosities 0.034-0.067 lb/ft/s, either hydrophobic (repel water after curing) or hydrophilic (continue to absorb water); and two-component polyurethanes (polyisocyanate and polyol), viscosities 0.067-0.67 lb/ft/s and strengths as high as 300 psi (Naudts 1995) (pp. 8-116 to 8-117).
key_points: Resins gel by polymerization or polycondensation; set time set by proportions
Used for very low viscosity, fast strength, variable set, chemical resistance or high groundwater flow

sections.title: Miscellaneous Grouts
sections.summary: Miscellaneous grouts (hot melts, latex, polyesters, epoxies, furanic resins, silicones, silacsols) give special qualities but may be limited by toxicity, handling and cost. Hot bitumen (low viscosity 0.01-0.034 lb/ft/s above about 400 F) is viable for challenging water-stopping, ideally with stable particulate grout; silacsols form stable calcium hydrosilicates, permanent and environmentally compatible in fine-medium sands.
sections.body: These grouts are essentially organic compounds or resins. Besides waterproofing and strengthening they provide specific qualities such as erosion or corrosion resistance and flexibility, but may be limited by toxicity, injection and handling difficulties, and cost. Categories include hot melts, latex, polyesters, epoxies, furanic resins, silicones and silacsols; polyesters and epoxies have little or no ground treatment application, and latex and furanic resins are very infrequently encountered. For certain seepage cut-offs, hot melts can be particularly viable. Bitumens are very high molecular weight hydrocarbons, usually petroleum distillation residues; viscous to hard at room temperature, they have relatively low viscosity (0.01 to 0.034 lb/ft/s) when hot (typically in excess of 400 F). Bitumen is used in particularly challenging water-stopping applications, remains stable with time and has good chemical resistance; contemporary practice requires simultaneous penetration of the placed bitumen by stable particulate grouts for good long-term performance (Bruce 2003). Silacsols are solution grouts formed by reacting an activated silica liquor with a calcium-based inorganic reagent; the products are calcium hydrosilicates with a crystalline structure similar to hydrated Portland cement, a direct molecular reaction rather than an evolutive gelation. Used since the mid-1980s with consistent success in fine-medium sands (Bruce 1988), the grout is stable, permanent and environmentally compatible, and compared with silica gels of similar rheology gives far lower permeability, far superior creep behavior of treated sands for grouts of similar strength (290 psi), and assured permanent filling even of unusually large pores or hydrofracture fissures (p. 8-117).
key_points: Categories: hot melts, latex, polyesters, epoxies, furanic resins, silicones, silacsols
Hot bitumen: viscosity 0.01-0.034 lb/ft/s when hot (typically above 400 F) (p. 8-117)
Bitumen should be penetrated simultaneously by stable particulate grout (Bruce 2003)
Silacsols: calcium hydrosilicate products; stable, permanent, environmentally compatible in fine-medium sands
