sections.title: Project Planning
sections.summary: Proper planning is essential for a successful grouting program, from project requirements and preliminary investigations through plans, specifications and design to post-construction monitoring, performance assessment, quality assurance and verification. Section 4 gives a suggested sequence of steps.
sections.body: Proper planning is essential for the completion of a successful grouting program. The planning process includes several phases, from determining project requirements, preliminary investigations, plans and specifications, and design, to post-construction monitoring, performance assessment, quality assurance and verification of the final product. This section gives grouting project users a suggested sequence of steps to plan and implement a successful grouting application (p. 8-118): seven planning steps (Section 4.1) and pregrouting subsurface investigations (Section 4.2).
key_points: Planning runs from requirements and investigation through design, monitoring and verification
Section 4.1 gives seven planning steps; Section 4.2 covers pregrouting investigations
sections.applicability: Planning a grouting project from requirements to verification.

sections.title: Project Planning Steps
sections.summary: Seven grouting project planning steps: (1) performance requirements; (2) adequacy of subsurface information; (3) general site conditions; (4) technical feasibility; (5) preliminary design and cost estimate; (6) specifications, contract documents and QA requirements; (7) construction monitoring and end results; summarized as designer and contractor responsibilities and shown in the decision flowchart (Figure 8-51).
sections.body: Section 4.1 lays out a sequence of seven steps for planning a grouting project: Step 1, determine project performance requirements; Step 2, assess the adequacy of the subsurface information; Step 3, identify and assess general site conditions; Step 4, technical feasibility; Step 5, preliminary design and cost estimates; Step 6, specifications, contract documents and quality assurance requirements; and Step 7, construction monitoring and end results (pp. 8-118 to 8-120). The steps are summarized as designer and contractor responsibilities, and the planning process is shown in the grouting decision flowchart, Figure 8-51 (pp. 8-120 to 8-121).
key_points: Seven steps from performance requirements to construction monitoring
Figure 8-51 is the grouting decision flowchart
sections.applicability: Following a structured planning sequence for a grouting project.

sections.title: Step 1: Determine Project Performance Requirements
sections.summary: Step 1: conduct a preliminary analysis of the desired qualitative and quantitative performance; define the extent of water control or waterproofing by measuring water flow and pressure, and the required structural improvement of soils or rocks in terms of compressive or shear strength or increased stiffness.
sections.body: To determine the requirements of the grouting activity, a preliminary analysis of the desired qualitative and quantitative levels of performance should be conducted. This should include the extent of water control or water proofing to be achieved by grouting, determined by measuring water flow and water pressure. The required structural improvement of the problematic geomaterial, soils and/or rocks, should be well defined in terms of compressive or shear strength or increased stiffness of the grout and the grouted mass (p. 8-118).
key_points: Define qualitative and quantitative performance levels
Water control target from measured water flow and pressure
Structural target as compressive or shear strength or stiffness of grout and grouted mass
sections.applicability: Setting measurable objectives for a grouting program.

sections.title: Step 2: Assess the Adequacy of the Subsurface Information
sections.summary: Step 2: using the Step 1 requirements, judge whether existing subsurface information defines the extent of the problem: treatment area and depth, variability of strata, and index and performance parameters to evaluate existing conditions and predicted performance before and after treatment.
sections.body: Based on the information assembled in Step 1, determine the adequacy of the existing subsurface information to assess the extent of the problematic condition. This would include the treatment area and depth as well as variability of the subsurface strata, and the index and performance parameters needed to evaluate existing conditions and the predicted performance before and following ground improvement treatment (p. 8-118).
key_points: Check whether existing data define treatment area and depth
Need strata variability and index/performance parameters before and after treatment
sections.applicability: Judging whether more site investigation is needed before grouting design.

sections.title: Step 3: Identify and Assess General Site Conditions
sections.summary: Step 3: investigate general site conditions before grouting design, including construction and operational space, existing overhead and subsurface structures, constructability and environmental constraints.
sections.body: General site conditions such as construction and operational space, existing structures (both overhead and sub-surface), constructability and environmental constraints should be investigated prior to design of the grouting program (p. 8-118). This is the third of the seven planning steps, following the definition of performance requirements and the assessment of subsurface information.
key_points: Assess working space, overhead and subsurface structures
Assess constructability and environmental constraints before design
sections.applicability: Site constraints to review before designing grouting.

sections.title: Step 4: Technical Feasibility
sections.summary: Step 4: identify all possible grouting solutions (permeation, jet or others) by technical feasibility, focused on expected outcomes; feasibility depends on existing geomaterial parameters and degree of improvement needed; consult specialists; plan qualitative and quantitative acceptance testing of the end product, recognizing success is hard to define quantitatively.
sections.body: All possible solutions to the problem, i.e., the applicable grouting types (permeation grouting, jet grouting or others), should be identified based on technical feasibility. This critical planning step should focus on the specific expectations and outcomes as far as possible. The feasibility of a grouting solution is directly related to the existing geomaterial parameters and the degree of improvement needed to meet the performance requirements; this is a good time to first consult specialists (consultants and/or contractors) (pp. 8-118 to 8-119). Another critical aspect is to evaluate the qualitative and quantitative methods that will be used to test the end product after grouting and accept the improved conditions. It is generally difficult to define success quantitatively; even when in situ or other field tests are used, they often require judgment and interpretation, while specifications and contract documents must be clear and specific (p. 8-119).
key_points: Identify all technically feasible grouting types
Feasibility depends on existing geomaterial parameters and degree of improvement needed
Consult specialists at this step
Decide how the end product will be tested and accepted; success is hard to define quantitatively
sections.applicability: Screening grouting methods for technical feasibility and acceptance testing.

sections.title: Step 5: Preliminary Design and Cost Estimates
sections.summary: Step 5: the owner prepares a preliminary design and cost estimate with a significant contingency for owner-directed scope changes and grout volumes from field monitoring. Table 8-12 lists grouting risks: schedule and budget (contracts, late notice, weather, access, materials, equipment, different site conditions) and geotechnical (slope instability, settlement, liquefaction, contamination, problem soils, impact on adjacent structures).
sections.body: The project owner must conduct a preliminary design to develop a preliminary cost estimate. Online guidance and the sections of this chapter give general guidance on design and cost. Even when comprehensive design information is available, the estimate should include a significant contingency percentage to address owner-directed changes in scope and grout volumes based on field monitoring of the contractor's means and methods. Risks of a grouting program and probable causes are listed in Table 8-12 (p. 8-119). Schedule and budget risk: contractual issues between general and specialty contractor; late notice to proceed; weather delays; site access problems; material supply and storage problems; equipment availability; different site conditions. Geotechnical issues and/or poor soil conditions: slope instability; settlement; liquefaction; contamination; problem soils, e.g., expansive clays; and impact on adjacent existing structures (p. 8-119).
key_points: Owner prepares preliminary design and cost estimate
Include a significant contingency for scope changes and grout volumes
Table 8-12 schedule/budget risks: contracts, late notice, weather, access, materials, equipment, site conditions
Table 8-12 geotechnical risks: slope instability, settlement, liquefaction, contamination, problem soils, adjacent structures
sections.applicability: Preliminary grouting cost estimates and risk register.

sections.title: Step 6: Specifications, Contract Documents and Quality Assurance Requirements
sections.summary: Step 6: contract documents are often performance-based with some means and methods controls, relying on the grouting contractor's qualifications (prequalification or documented experience). QA should cover the contractor's QC of grout material, grout pipes and placement; contractor sampling and testing, with an outside agency engaged and owner independent testing.
sections.body: The design of a grouting project requires contracting documents that are often written in a performance-based specification format, typically including some means and methods controls but largely relying on the qualifications and experience of the grouting specialty contractor. The specifications should include prequalification requirements or a documented experience record as a submittal following award. Quality assurance requirements should address the contractor's quality control procedures for the principal grouting aspects: grout material, grout pipe drilling, and placement of the grout. The contractor is also often responsible for sampling and testing to assure the end product meets the performance requirements, but an outside agency should be engaged; the owner may also conduct independent testing and monitoring to validate that the contractor followed the proposed QA process (p. 8-120).
key_points: Performance-based specifications with some means and methods controls
Require contractor prequalification or a documented experience record
QA covers grout material, grout pipe drilling and grout placement
Engage an outside agency; owner may test independently
sections.applicability: Writing grouting specifications and QA requirements.

sections.title: Step 7: Construction Monitoring and End Results
sections.summary: Step 7: the owner should actively monitor progress and evaluate results in real time, changing acceptance procedures or means and methods if needed, often through an outside consultant. Steps summarized as designer and contractor responsibilities; planning shown in the grouting decision flowchart (Figure 8-51).
sections.body: The owner should be actively involved in monitoring progress and schedule during construction and evaluating the results of the grouting program, to determine in real time whether interim results and testing meet expectations and, if not, to change acceptance procedures or the contractor's means and methods; an outside consultant is often employed for this. The steps are summarized as designer and contractor responsibilities: establishing specific objectives (designer); defining the geometric and geotechnical project conditions and the properties of the treated soil/rock (designer); developing the grouting program design, companion specifications and contract documents (designer); planning grouting equipment and procedural approach (contractor); and monitoring and evaluation of the program (designer, contractor). The planning process is shown in the flowchart in Figure 8-51 (pp. 8-120 to 8-121).
key_points: Owner monitors progress and results in real time
Change acceptance procedures or means and methods when interim results fall short
Designer: objectives, conditions, design and documents; contractor: equipment and procedures; both: monitoring
figures: Figure 8-51: Grouting decision flowchart.
sections.applicability: Owner oversight of grouting construction and acceptance.

sections.title: Pregrouting Subsurface Investigations
sections.summary: Pregrouting investigations need more borings than usual, continuous samples and lab tests (grain size, density, permeability, pH, index properties); define stratigraphy (micro-layers, silt lenses), site history and anomalies. Groundwater pH matters: high pH destroys silicate grouts, low pH harms Portland cement grouts and stops acrylamide/acrylate setting; organics affect gel times. Run grout mixing tests with site groundwater.
sections.body: Pregrouting subsurface investigation programs normally require more than the usual number of borings and should include continuous samples and laboratory tests, including grain size, density, permeability, pH and other index properties. The purpose is to define the limits and characteristics of the geotechnical situation to be solved, and equally to identify the geological conditions that will control and permit success: stratigraphy, environment and groundwater regime (p. 8-121). Stratigraphy, the variation in permeability, strength and density in the grouting zone, is an important controlling factor; a higher sampling frequency should identify micro-layers, silt layers and fine-grained lenses, with gradation curves. Site history must be evaluated, and anomalies such as unexpected changes in drilling or grouting or in effluent pH recorded. Groundwater pH should be measured: high pH can be very destructive to sodium silicate grouts, preventing gel formation and/or causing degradation, while very low pH soils can be very destructive to Portland cement grouts; low pH can also accelerate silicate setting while preventing the setting of acrylamide or acrylate grouts and inhibiting cementitious reactions. Organic materials in the ground or groundwater can dramatically affect gel times and quality of chemical and cement grouts. Chemical analysis of groundwater is useful but should not replace at least one series of grout mixing tests using groundwater from the site (p. 8-122).
key_points: More borings than usual, continuous samples, lab tests (grain size, density, permeability, pH, index)
Sample frequently to find micro-layers, silt layers and fine-grained lenses
High groundwater pH destroys silicate grouts; very low pH harms Portland cement grouts
Low pH prevents setting of acrylamide/acrylate grouts
Organics affect gel times and grout quality
Do at least one series of grout mixing tests with site groundwater (p. 8-122)
sections.applicability: Scoping site investigations for grouting design.

sections.title: Construction Specifications and Quality Assurance
sections.summary: Introduces Section 5 on developing specifications for grouting projects: specification types, bid items and estimating quantities, guide specification outlines for each grouting technique, inspection and verification, quality assurance and instrumentation monitoring.
sections.body: Development of specifications for grouting projects is described in this section (p. 8-123). It covers specification development (prescriptive and performance types), bid items and methods of estimating quantities, guide specification outlines for permeation, compaction, jet and rock grouting, void filling and slabjacking, inspection control and verification, quality assurance, and instrumentation monitoring and construction control.
key_points: Covers specification types, bid items, guide specification outlines, inspection, QA and monitoring
sections.applicability: Preparing specifications and QA provisions for grouting contracts.

sections.title: Specification Development
sections.summary: Grouting specifications are prescriptive (strict procedural, monitoring and material rules; promote low bids, discourage innovation) or performance (contractor achieves defined criteria and may modify design and methods). Technical specification items per Weaver and Bruce (2007): mobilization/demobilization, drilling and redrilling, special flushing, water pressure testing, grouting, standby; the contractor prepares a Method Statement.
sections.body: Primary reference: Specifications for Rock Mass Grouting (Bruce and Dreese 2010). Grouting specifications can be classified as prescriptive or performance specifications. Prescriptive specifications consist of regulatory procedural, supervisory, monitoring and material use rules that the contractor must strictly follow; they promote low-bid situations and discourage innovative engineering. Performance specifications require the contractor to achieve pre-defined performance criteria for the final product, allowing modification of design, construction and performance of project components. Grouting involves specialized equipment, materials, procedures, personnel and pay items, so specification development needs highly skilled and experienced contractors and efficient contractor-owner communication. The tasks and responsibilities to be allocated beforehand are enumerated by Weaver and Bruce (2007), which also tabulates the items to be addressed in the technical specification: mobilization/demobilization/general; drilling and redrilling; special flushing; water pressure testing; grouting; and standby (owner rights and personnel). The contractor prepares a detailed Method Statement (working plan) consistent with the specification and describing all phases of work; the specification and Method Statement govern the owner's supervision and monitoring. Performance specifications let contractors offer alternative approaches, materials or equipment to achieve the desired performance (p. 8-123).
key_points: Prescriptive specifications: strict rules; promote low bids, discourage innovation
Performance specifications: contractor meets defined criteria and may modify methods
Technical specification items: mobilization, drilling/redrilling, special flushing, water pressure testing, grouting, standby
Contractor prepares a Method Statement (working plan)
sections.applicability: Choosing between prescriptive and performance grouting specifications.

sections.title: Bid Items
sections.summary: Container for grouting bid items: methods of estimating quantities (test grouting, subsurface evaluation, unit-take estimates, experience) and the bid items to include in a drilling and grouting schedule.
sections.body: This section covers how quantities for a drilling and grouting program are estimated (Section 5.2.1) and the bid items experience shows should be included in any estimate or bid schedule (Section 5.2.2), from mobilization and environmental protection through drilling, pressure washing and testing, grout placement, connections, materials and injection parameter recording (pp. 8-124 to 8-126).
key_points: 5.2.1 estimating quantities; 5.2.2 bid items
sections.applicability: Structuring the bid schedule of a grouting contract.

sections.title: Methods of Estimating Quantities
sections.summary: Grouting quantities are estimated by test grouting (most reliable for medium and large projects, preferably in design, on a representative site with production methods), evaluation of subsurface samples and water pressure tests, 'unit take' estimates over reaches and zones, and local experience as a reality check.
sections.body: Test grouting: for medium and large projects, probably the most reliable way to estimate quantities is a test-grouting program, preferably during design; the test site should be geologically representative of what was found in exploration, and the means, methods and materials must be substantially those envisaged for production. Evaluation of subsurface information: evaluating samples, water pressure tests and other tests is a fundamental part of preparing a grouting estimate, with care for site variability and technical complexity. 'Unit take' estimates: a method often used for detailed estimates, in which the area is divided into horizontal reaches and vertical zones of varying properties based on site geology and in-situ tests, and the number of primary and split-spaced holes needed for each area and zone is estimated. Experience: local knowledge of contractors or engineers is invaluable as a 'reality check' on quantities derived by other methods (p. 8-124).
key_points: Test grouting is probably most reliable for medium and large projects
Test site must be geologically representative; use production means and materials
Unit take: divide area into reaches and zones, estimate primary and split-spaced holes
Local experience provides a reality check
sections.applicability: Estimating drilling and grout quantities for bidding.

sections.title: Bid Items
sections.summary: Recommended grouting bid items: mobilization/demobilization (lump sum, guaranteed); environmental protection (lump sum); drilling grout holes per linear foot (separate items by diameter, depth, angle; redrilling typically 50% of rock drilling rate); pressure washing and testing by time; grout placement by volume or pump hour; connections per hookup; grout materials by volume or weight; injection parameter recording and analysis paid separately.
sections.body: Experience indicates the following items should be in any estimate or bid schedule for drilling and grouting. Mobilization and demobilization, lump sum: equipment must be assembled and removed regardless of the work done, so a separate item guarantees payment (p. 8-124). Environmental protection, lump sum: retention of the environment in its natural state as far as possible. Drilling grout holes, per linear foot (rock, soil, grout): a minimum diameter is generally specified; separate items for different diameters, depths, angles or special conditions such as galleries; redrilling set grout through no fault of the contractor typically paid at 50% of the rock drilling rate. Pressure washing and pressure testing: preliminary washing is part of drilling, but pressure washing and testing are paid separately, measured by time, and may be combined in one item. Grout placement, by volume or pump hour: labor, equipment and supplies (other than materials) to mix and inject. Connections to grout holes, lump sum or per connection: hookup labor is independent of placement (p. 8-125). Grout materials, by volume or weight: separate items for each material except water, estimated from experience, geology and test grouting, consistent with placement volumes. Grout injection parameter recording and analysis: where warranted, the computer-based system is paid separately as a lump sum or weekly or monthly fixed cost (p. 8-126).
key_points: Mobilization/demobilization as a guaranteed lump sum
Drilling per linear ft; separate items by diameter, depth, angle or special conditions
Redrilling set grout typically 50% of the rock drilling rate (p. 8-125)
Pressure washing and testing paid separately by time
Grout placement by volume or pump hour; materials by volume or weight (except water)
Computer monitoring paid separately as lump sum or recurring fixed cost (p. 8-126)
sections.applicability: Writing the bid item list for a drilling and grouting contract.

sections.title: Specifications
sections.summary: Grouting specifications must be tailored to project objectives, avoiding 'cut and paste'; no standard specification fits all grouting. Guide specification outlines from ASCE and experienced contractors follow for permeation, compaction, jet and rock grouting, void filling and slabjacking.
sections.body: Specifications for grouting projects must be tailored to the specific objectives of the project, with caution about 'cut and paste' efforts. Performance requirements, site conditions, design specifications and economic considerations all play an important role. No standard specifications exist that are directly applicable to all types of grouting project, so it is important to understand the specification items associated with each type of grouting. Guide specifications by ASCE and experienced grouting contractors are provided in the subsections for permeation, compaction, jet and rock grouting, void filling and slabjacking (p. 8-126).
key_points: Tailor specifications to project objectives; avoid cut-and-paste
No standard specification fits all grouting types
Guide outlines given for six grouting types
sections.applicability: Starting points for grouting specifications by technique.

sections.title: Permeation Grouting Specifications
sections.summary: Outline of a contractor-developed guide specification for permeation grouting: General (introduction, intent, standards, definitions, scope, submittals, QA), Equipment and Materials (grouting equipment, grout pipes, grout materials), Execution (site examination and preparation, permeation grouting, mixing, injection, field QC, testing and inspection, restrictions), Payment.
sections.body: Guide specifications developed by a specialty grouting contractor for permeation grouting are presented; to develop performance specifications for permeation or chemical grouting it may be necessary to add or remove items so all project requirements are met (p. 8-126). The outline is: 1. General: introduction; intent; standards and references; definitions; scope of work; submittals; quality assurance. 2. Equipment and Materials: grouting equipment; grout pipes; grout materials. 3. Execution: site examination; site preparation; permeation grouting; grouting mixing method; injection procedures; field quality control; testing and inspection; restrictions. 4. Payment: method of payment (pp. 8-126 to 8-127).
key_points: Four parts: General, Equipment and Materials, Execution, Payment
Add or remove items to suit project requirements
sections.applicability: Outline for a permeation or chemical grouting specification.

sections.title: Compaction Grouting Specifications
sections.summary: Outline of the ASCE compaction grouting guide (ASCE 2010): scope, access, treatment area and depth, utilities, materials, drilling and grouting equipment, data acquisition and real-time monitoring, communication, order of work, drilling, grout injection (sequence, staging, injection rate, refusal criteria on pressure, displacement and volume, grout jacking), site restoration and submittals.
sections.body: Guide specifications for compaction grouting developed by ASCE are presented (ASCE 2010). The outline is: 1. Scope of work; 2. Access and site conditions; 3. Treatment area and depth; 4. Subsurface pipes and utilities; 5. Materials (grout mixture, cement, aggregates, water); 6. Drilling and grouting equipment (drilling equipment, grout casing, casing withdrawal system, grout batcher/mixer, grout pump, delivery line, pressure gauges); 7. Data acquisition and reporting (logged information, real-time computer monitoring, daily report, movement monitoring system); 8. Communication system; 9. Order of work; 10. Drilling (establishing grout holes, hole location, control of drilling circulation flush, water injection, drilling log); 11. Grout injection (depth confirmation, sequence, grout staging, access requirements, injection rate, grout refusal criteria: duration of pumping at maximum specified header pressure, sustained pumping at maximum header pressure, limit allowable displacement of adjacent structure, limit unwanted displacement of the ground surface during a stage, limit grout volume injected; improperly grouted holes; grout jacking; hole completion); 12. Site maintenance and restoration; 13. Submittals (grouting plan, monitoring procedures) (pp. 8-127 to 8-129).
key_points: Based on ASCE (2010) compaction grouting consensus guide
Includes real-time computer monitoring and movement monitoring
Refusal criteria: pressure duration, sustained pressure, structure displacement, ground displacement, grout volume
sections.applicability: Outline for a compaction grouting specification.

sections.title: Jet Grouting Specifications
sections.summary: Outline of the ASCE jet grouting guideline (ASCE 2009): qualifications, submittals (equipment, mix design, field demonstration test, procedure, QA/QC), materials and equipment, execution (test program, production, QC/QA), acceptance criteria (repeat test parameters, minimum 85% core recovery, permeability, minimum 28-day strength, overlap, verticality), measurement and payment by lump sum and coring per foot.
sections.body: Guide specifications for jet grouting were developed by ASCE (ASCE 2009). 1. General: scope, project objectives and job site conditions; references; definitions; qualifications (project and personnel experience); submittals (qualifications, jet grouting equipment, grout mix design, field demonstration test program, jet grouting procedure, QA/QC and verification procedures for field test and production work, daily reports). 2. Materials and Equipment: cement, slag, fly ash, potable water, bentonite and component ratios; general, drilling, grout mixing and injection equipment, jet grouting pump, compressor, filling grout pump, jet grout tools and equipment instrumentation. 3. Execution: test program; production work; quality control/quality assurance; daily reports; acceptance criteria: accurate repetition of test program parameters; minimum core recovery of 85%, subject to coring penetration rate, overall integrity and presence of gravel below jet-grouted soil; permeability; minimum 28-day compressive strength of jet grout samples (grout only); minimum overlap thickness; verticality and horizontal tolerances. 4. Measurement and Payment: mobilization, test program including verification testing, and jet grouting measured and paid as lump sums; coring for verification per linear foot per hole (pp. 8-129 to 8-131).
key_points: Based on the ASCE (2009) jet grouting guideline
Submittals include a field demonstration test program and QA/QC procedures
Acceptance: repeat test parameters, minimum 85% core recovery, permeability, minimum 28-day strength, overlap, verticality
Mobilization, test program and jet grouting paid as lump sums; coring per linear ft per hole
sections.applicability: Outline for a jet grouting specification and acceptance criteria.

sections.title: Rock Grouting Specifications
sections.summary: Rock fissure grouting specification items and payment methods (Weaver and Bruce 2007): mobilization/demobilization (lump sum, typically 50-60% on mobilization), drilling and redrilling (per linear foot, reduced redrilling rate), special flushing (per crew hour), water-pressure testing (per crew hour or per test), grouting (per pump hour, per kg or lb of materials, possibly monthly QA/QC; e.g., paddle mixers and w/c > 2 by weight unacceptable), standby (per crew hour).
sections.body: Weaver and Bruce (2007) suggested items and tasks to define in technical specifications for rock fissure grouting (p. 8-131). Mobilization and demobilization: lump sum (typically 50-60% on mobilization, balance on demobilization); project phases, duration restraints, site location, facilities on arrival and for others, site preparation (grout caps, access roads, scaffolding). Drilling and redrilling: per linear foot, with a reduced redrilling rate for hardened grout; hole quantities, location, length, orientation and inclination; stage length and method (upstage vs. downstage); minimum diameter; unacceptable events (e.g., air flush in rock); special methods; deviation tolerances and measurement; actions for extreme events (major flush loss, rod drops); logging; environmental restrictions; standpipes or casing; routine washing (pp. 8-131 to 8-132). Special flushing: per crew hour; purpose, duration and method, pressure and flow limits, flushing aids, spoils. Water-pressure testing: per crew hour for multiple-pressure or extended tests, per test for simple short (e.g., 5 to 10 minute) tests; purpose, limits, durations, upstage vs. downstage, data recording and analysis, investigatory and verification testing. Grouting: per pump hour, per kilogram (or lb) of materials and possibly per month for specified QA/QC monitoring; stage length and method, sequencing to closure, delays between adjacent holes, pressures and flow rates, refusal criteria, preconstruction testing, QA/QC, data accuracy, mix properties and plan to change them, unusual situations (runaway takes, zero takes, interconnections, surface leaks), equipment, unacceptable methods (e.g., paddle mixers, w/c ratio > 2 by weight), materials, backfilling, relation of drilling and permeability testing to takes, communication (pp. 8-132 to 8-133). Standby: per crew hour; circumstances under which the owner instructs, crew size and composition (p. 8-133).
key_points: Mobilization lump sum, typically 50-60% paid on mobilization
Drilling per linear ft with reduced rate for redrilling hardened grout; air flush in rock unacceptable
Water-pressure testing per crew hour, or per test for simple 5-10 minute tests
Grouting per pump hour and per kg/lb of materials; refusal criteria and closure sequencing specified
Unacceptable: paddle mixers, w/c ratio > 2 by weight (p. 8-133)
Standby per crew hour

sections.title: Void Filling Specifications
sections.summary: Void fill grouting lacks performance-based specifications for transportation; method specifications for bulk infill of old mines exist (Healy and Head 1984). A state DOT guide specification for concrete-filled geotextile forms for scour repair (Welsh 1997) is given: woven geotextile tubes or bags with self-sealing valves, height not more than half the width, Table 8-13 properties, stainless steel dowels embedded 1 ft into each bag.
sections.body: Void fill grouting currently lacks acceptable performance-based specifications for direct application to transportation projects. Method specifications developed by Healy and Head (1984) for bulk infill grouting of old mines serve as a guide; both kinds of specification should be tailored to site conditions. The guide specification given was developed by a state transportation department for scour repair (p. 8-133). Guide Specification, Concrete Filled Forms for Scour Repair (Welsh 1997): the item governs construction of concrete-filled containers for scour repair per the plans or as established by the Engineer. Synthetic textile forms are used; units are pumped in place, with connecting dowels for interlock between tubes or bags. Containers should be woven geotextile from stabilized yarns, designed to remedy each scour zone singly or as a group, with at least one self-sealing valve; where void dimensions are uncertain, tubes and bags should be field sewn so the inflated height is not more than one-half of the width. The geotextile must meet Table 8-13, which lists, among others, grab tensile strength (ASTM D4632) 320 warp - 300 fill lbf, grab elongation 18 warp - 22 fill %, burst strength (ASTM D3786) 625 psi, trapezoidal tear (ASTM D4522) 130 warp - 130 fill lbf, puncture (ASTM D4833) 80 lbf, coefficient of permeability 0.9 in./s and permittivity 1.5 1/sec (ASTM D4491) (pp. 8-134 to 8-135). Reinforcing dowels, if required, are stainless steel or approved equal, embedded at least 0.3 m (1 ft) into the lower bag and protruding 0.3 m (1 ft) into the upper bag, spaced one meter apart in tubes (p. 8-135).
key_points: No performance-based void fill specifications for transportation; method specifications for mines (Healy and Head 1984)
Scour repair: woven geotextile tubes/bags with at least one self-sealing valve
Inflated container height not more than one-half of its width
Table 8-13: grab tensile 320 warp/300 fill lbf; burst 625 psi; puncture 80 lbf; permittivity 1.5 1/sec
Dowels embedded at least 1 ft into lower and upper bags; 1 m spacing in tubes

sections.title: Slabjacking Specifications
sections.summary: The guide specification UFGS-32 01 29.62 (USACE 2008) covers slabjacking rigid pavements for roads, streets, parking, airfields and general uses, editable to suit the project. Outline: General (unit prices, submittals, QA), Products (equipment, grout mixture, materials, tests), Execution (drilling, washing, jacking, raising, sealing holes, grade, acceptance).
sections.body: The guide specification UFGS-32 01 29.62 (USACE 2008) covers the requirements for slabjacking rigid pavements for roads, streets, parking areas, airfields and other general applications; it may be edited by adding, deleting or revising text to suit the project (p. 8-135). Outline: 1. General: unit prices (measurement of the quantity of Portland cement grout, quantity of Portland cement, number of holes, broken slabs; payment by Portland cement unit price and drilled holes); references; submittals; quality assurance (bench marks, testing facilities, cement, aggregate); delivery, storage and handling; environmental requirements. 2. Products: executing equipment (grout plant, water tanker, drilling, flow cone, miscellaneous); grout mixture; mineral aggregate (particle shape, grading, deleterious materials); pozzolans and fly ash; Portland cement; water; chemical admixtures; proportioning; tests, inspections and verifications (daily report, compressive strength, expansion, set time, fluidity). 3. Execution: pavement inspection; drilling holes for grout injection; wash holes; jacking; raising of slabs; sealing of injection holes; plan grade requirements; replacing and repair of damaged pavement; production sampling and testing (aggregates, field test specimens); protection of pavement; acceptance of work (pp. 8-135 to 8-137).

Payment by Portland cement unit price and drilled holes
Tests: compressive strength, expansion, set time, fluidity
Execution covers drilling, washing, jacking, raising, sealing holes and grade requirements

sections.title: Inspection Control and Verification
sections.summary: Void filling and slabjacking tend to need one-of-a-kind solutions, so guide specifications are difficult; the engineer should use the preceding specifications as a guide. The bidding method depends on what is known about the problem, ranging from cost-plus to lump sum.
sections.body: Void filling and slabjacking problems tend to necessitate 'one-of-a-kind' grouting solutions, which makes a guide specification difficult. It is suggested that the engineer developing the specification and construction control use the preceding specifications as a guide. The bidding method will also depend on the amount of knowledge available about the problem: information on the problem and its potential solution will determine the actual bidding method and the risks placed on the grouting contractor, which can range from cost-plus through a lump-sum method (pp. 8-137 to 8-138).
key_points: Void filling and slabjacking need one-of-a-kind solutions
Use the preceding guide specifications as a guide
Bidding ranges from cost-plus to lump sum depending on knowledge of the problem
sections.applicability: Construction control and bidding for void filling and slabjacking.

sections.title: Quality Assurance
sections.summary: Grouting QA relies on drill logs, test results and grout pressure/volume/time records studied in real time so the program can be adjusted; higher order holes should take less grout than primaries. Monitor fluid properties (fluidity, specific gravity, set time, stability; slump for compaction grouting); baseline the site before grouting; verify after; run preconstruction test programs.
sections.body: Effective QA based on well-developed testing and performance criteria is essential. Every drill hole is a potential source of information, and drill logs and test results, manual or electronic, provide valuable data; the key is that data are studied in real time or soon after so the program can be adjusted promptly. Grouting data likewise show how the ground responds: close examination of grout pressure/volume/time records gives vital insight into effectiveness; for example, in a well-progressing rock grouting operation, higher order holes have smaller grout takes and need slower injection at equivalent pressures to reach refusal than the primaries. During grouting the fluid properties of the injected materials must be monitored frequently: for rock fissure or soil permeation grouting, record fluidity, specific gravity, setting time and stability; for compaction grouting only slump testing may be relevant. The site's geotechnical situation must be 'baselined' before grouting, measuring key virgin parameters (such as density or permeability), and verification testing reflecting the project goals must follow the work. Grouting has a great need for preconstruction test programs, letting the designer's assumptions and contractor's methods be tried and verified before production; this is often overlooked (p. 8-138).
key_points: Study drilling and grouting data in real time and adjust the program promptly
Higher order holes should show smaller takes than primaries if grouting is progressing well
Rock/permeation grouting: monitor fluidity, specific gravity, set time, stability; compaction: slump
Baseline key parameters (density, permeability) before grouting; verify afterward
Run preconstruction test programs
sections.applicability: Quality assurance and verification of grouting work.

sections.title: Instrumentation Monitoring and Construction Control
sections.summary: Monitoring instrumentation for accurate and sufficient field data is essential; the required level of monitoring and responsibilities are typically quality control items in the specifications, developed specifically for each project because techniques differ in equipment, design and testing.
sections.body: Monitoring the instrumentation for accuracy and sufficiency of field-collected data is essential for the success of any grouting project. The required level of monitoring and the responsibilities for it are typically included as quality control items in the specifications. Since different grouting techniques require different types of equipment, design and testing methods, monitoring activities should be developed specifically for each project (p. 8-139).
key_points: Accurate, sufficient field data are essential
Monitoring level and responsibilities go in the specifications as QC items
Develop monitoring specifically for each project and technique
sections.applicability: Planning instrumentation and construction control for grouting.
